Now, fair Hippolyta, our nuptial hour / Draws on apace; four happy days bring in / Another moon; but oh, methinks, how slow / This old moon wanes! She lingers my desires, / Like to a step-dame or a dowager, / Long withering out a young man's revenue.

Now, beautiful Hippolyta, our wedding day is coming fast. In four happy days there will be a new moon. But oh, how slowly this old moon seems to fade! She keeps me waiting for what I want, like a stepmother or a widow who lives on and on, eating up the money a young heir is waiting to inherit.

Four days will quickly steep themselves in night; / Four nights will quickly dream away the time; / And then the moon, like to a silver bow / New bent in heaven, shall behold the night / Of our solemnities.
Four days will quickly sink into night, and four nights will quickly pass in dreams. Then the new moon, like a silver bow freshly bent in the sky, will look down on the night of our wedding.
Go, Philostrate, / Stir up the Athenian youth to merriments; / Awake the pert and nimble spirit of mirth; / Turn melancholy forth to funerals; / The pale companion is not for our pomp.

Go, Philostrate, get the young people of Athens ready to celebrate. Wake up the lively, quick spirit of fun. Send sadness off to funerals, where it belongs. That pale-faced companion has no place at our festivities.
Hippolyta, I woo'd thee with my sword, / And won thy love doing thee injuries; / But I will wed thee in another key, / With pomp, with triumph, and with revelling.
Hippolyta, I courted you with my sword, and won your love by doing you harm in battle. But I will marry you in a different style: with grand shows, with public celebrations, and with partying.
Happy be Theseus, our renownèd Duke!
Long life and happiness to Theseus, our famous Duke!
Thanks, good Egeus. What's the news with thee?
Thank you, good Egeus. What news do you bring?

Full of vexation come I, with complaint / Against my child, my daughter Hermia. / Stand forth, Demetrius. My noble lord, / This man hath my consent to marry her. / Stand forth, Lysander. And, my gracious Duke, / This man hath bewitch'd the bosom of my child. / Thou, thou, Lysander, thou hast given her rhymes, / And interchang'd love-tokens with my child. / Thou hast by moonlight at her window sung, / With feigning voice, verses of feigning love; / And stol'n the impression of her fantasy / With bracelets of thy hair, rings, gauds, conceits, / Knacks, trifles, nosegays, sweetmeats (messengers / Of strong prevailment in unharden'd youth) / With cunning hast thou filch'd my daughter's heart, / Turn'd her obedience (which is due to me) / To stubborn harshness. And, my gracious Duke, / Be it so she will not here before your grace / Consent to marry with Demetrius, / I beg the ancient privilege of Athens: / As she is mine I may dispose of her; / Which shall be either to this gentleman / Or to her death, according to our law / Immediately provided in that case.

I come here full of anger, to complain about my own child, my daughter Hermia. Step forward, Demetrius. My noble lord, this man has my permission to marry her. Step forward, Lysander. And, my gracious Duke, this man has put a spell on my child's heart. You, you, Lysander, you have given her poems and swapped love-tokens with her. You have sung at her window by moonlight in a fake, sweet voice, singing verses of fake love. You have stolen her imagination with bracelets made of your hair, rings, cheap toys, trinkets, little gifts, flowers and sweets, which are powerful persuaders for a young girl who knows no better. With your tricks you have stolen my daughter's heart, and turned the obedience she owes me into stubbornness. So, my gracious Duke, if she will not agree here, in front of you, to marry Demetrius, I ask for the old right of every Athenian father. Since she belongs to me, I may do what I like with her: either give her to this gentleman or have her put to death, as our law clearly lays down for this case.

What say you, Hermia? Be advis'd, fair maid. / To you your father should be as a god; / One that compos'd your beauties, yea, and one / To whom you are but as a form in wax / By him imprinted, and within his power / To leave the figure, or disfigure it. / Demetrius is a worthy gentleman.

What do you say, Hermia? Think carefully, pretty girl. Your father should be like a god to you. He made your beauty. To him you are like a wax figure he has shaped, and he has the power to leave the figure as it is or to destroy it. Demetrius is a fine gentleman.
In himself he is. / But in this kind, wanting your father's voice, / The other must be held the worthier.
As a man, he is. But in this matter, since he does not have your father's support, the other man must be considered the better one.
I would my father look'd but with my eyes.
I wish my father could see with my eyes.
Rather your eyes must with his judgment look.
Instead, your eyes must see with his judgement.

I do entreat your Grace to pardon me. / I know not by what power I am made bold, / Nor how it may concern my modesty / In such a presence here to plead my thoughts: / But I beseech your Grace that I may know / The worst that may befall me in this case, / If I refuse to wed Demetrius.

I beg your Grace to forgive me. I don't know what has made me so bold, or whether it is proper for a girl to speak her mind in front of such great people. But please tell me the worst that can happen to me if I refuse to marry Demetrius.

Either to die the death, or to abjure / For ever the society of men. / Therefore, fair Hermia, question your desires, / Know of your youth, examine well your blood, / Whether, if you yield not to your father's choice, / You can endure the livery of a nun, / For aye to be in shady cloister mew'd, / To live a barren sister all your life, / Chanting faint hymns to the cold fruitless moon. / Thrice-blessèd they that master so their blood / To undergo such maiden pilgrimage, / But earthlier happy is the rose distill'd / Than that which, withering on the virgin thorn, / Grows, lives, and dies, in single blessedness.

Either you will be put to death, or you must give up the company of men for ever. So, beautiful Hermia, think hard about what you want. Remember how young you are, and test your feelings, to decide whether, if you refuse your father's choice, you can bear to wear a nun's robes, to be shut up for ever in a gloomy convent, to live your whole life as a childless sister, singing weak hymns to the cold, barren moon. Those who can control their passions enough to live like that, as pure as pilgrims, are blessed three times over. But on earth a rose that is picked and made into perfume is happier than one that withers on its untouched stem, and grows, lives and dies alone.
So will I grow, so live, so die, my lord, / Ere I will yield my virgin patent up / Unto his lordship, whose unwishèd yoke / My soul consents not to give sovereignty.
Then I will grow, live and die that way, my lord, before I give up my freedom to a man whose rule over me I never wanted, and whom my soul refuses to accept as master.

Take time to pause; and by the next new moon / The sealing-day betwixt my love and me / For everlasting bond of fellowship, / Upon that day either prepare to die / For disobedience to your father's will, / Or else to wed Demetrius, as he would, / Or on Diana's altar to protest / For aye austerity and single life.

Take time to think. By the next new moon, the day my love and I are joined together for ever, on that day you must either prepare to die for disobeying your father, or marry Demetrius as he wishes, or swear at the altar of Diana, goddess of chastity, to live a strict and single life for ever.
Relent, sweet Hermia; and, Lysander, yield / Thy crazèd title to my certain right.
Give in, sweet Hermia. And, Lysander, give up your crazy claim to what is rightfully mine.
You have her father's love, Demetrius. / Let me have Hermia's. Do you marry him.
You have her father's love, Demetrius. Let me have Hermia's. Why don't you marry him?
Scornful Lysander, true, he hath my love; / And what is mine my love shall render him; / And she is mine, and all my right of her / I do estate unto Demetrius.
Rude Lysander! It's true he has my love, and because I love him I will give him what is mine. She is mine, and I hand over all my rights in her to Demetrius.

I am, my lord, as well deriv'd as he, / As well possess'd; my love is more than his; / My fortunes every way as fairly rank'd, / If not with vantage, as Demetrius'; / And, which is more than all these boasts can be, / I am belov'd of beauteous Hermia. / Why should not I then prosecute my right? / Demetrius, I'll avouch it to his head, / Made love to Nedar's daughter, Helena, / And won her soul; and she, sweet lady, dotes, / Devoutly dotes, dotes in idolatry, / Upon this spotted and inconstant man.

My lord, I come from as good a family as he does, and I am as rich. I love her more than he does. In every way my prospects are as good as his, if not better. And, more important than any of these boasts, beautiful Hermia loves me. So why shouldn't I claim what is mine? I'll say it to his face: Demetrius courted Nedar's daughter, Helena, and won her heart. And she, sweet lady, adores him, worships him like an idol, this stained and unfaithful man.

I must confess that I have heard so much, / And with Demetrius thought to have spoke thereof; / But, being over-full of self-affairs, / My mind did lose it.—But, Demetrius, come, / And come, Egeus; you shall go with me. / I have some private schooling for you both.— / For you, fair Hermia, look you arm yourself / To fit your fancies to your father's will, / Or else the law of Athens yields you up / (Which by no means we may extenuate) / To death, or to a vow of single life. / Come, my Hippolyta. What cheer, my love? / Demetrius and Egeus, go along; / I must employ you in some business / Against our nuptial, and confer with you / Of something nearly that concerns yourselves.

I must admit I have heard as much, and meant to speak to Demetrius about it, but I was so busy with my own affairs that I forgot. But Demetrius, come, and Egeus, come too. You will come with me. I have some private advice for you both. As for you, beautiful Hermia, make sure you bring your wishes into line with your father's will, or else the law of Athens, which I have no power to soften, will condemn you to death or to a life alone. Come, my Hippolyta. Are you all right, my love? Demetrius and Egeus, come along. I need your help with some arrangements for our wedding, and I want to talk to you about something that closely concerns you both.
With duty and desire we follow you.
We follow you out of duty and gladly.
How now, my love? Why is your cheek so pale? / How chance the roses there do fade so fast?
What is it, my love? Why are your cheeks so pale? How is it that the roses there are fading so fast?
Belike for want of rain, which I could well / Beteem them from the tempest of my eyes.
Probably because they need rain, which I could easily give them from the storm in my eyes.
Ay me! For aught that I could ever read, / Could ever hear by tale or history, / The course of true love never did run smooth. / But either it was different in blood—
Oh dear! From everything I have ever read, or heard in stories or history, the course of true love never ran smoothly. Either the lovers were from different social classes...
O cross! Too high to be enthrall'd to low.
What a misery! To be too high-born to be tied to someone low!
Or else misgraffèd in respect of years—
Or they were badly matched in age...
O spite! Too old to be engag'd to young.
How cruel! To be too old to be engaged to someone young!
Or else it stood upon the choice of friends—
Or else it depended on the choice of family and friends...
O hell! to choose love by another's eyes!
Oh, hell! To choose a lover through someone else's eyes!

Or, if there were a sympathy in choice, / War, death, or sickness did lay siege to it, / Making it momentany as a sound, / Swift as a shadow, short as any dream, / Brief as the lightning in the collied night / That, in a spleen, unfolds both heaven and earth, / And, ere a man hath power to say, 'Behold!' / The jaws of darkness do devour it up: / So quick bright things come to confusion.

Or, if the lovers did suit each other, war, death or illness attacked their love and made it last only a moment, like a sound, as quick as a shadow, as short as a dream, as brief as lightning on a pitch-black night, which in a flash lights up heaven and earth, and before anyone can say 'Look!' the jaws of darkness swallow it up. That's how quickly bright things are destroyed.

If then true lovers have ever cross'd, / It stands as an edict in destiny. / Then let us teach our trial patience, / Because it is a customary cross, / As due to love as thoughts and dreams and sighs, / Wishes and tears, poor fancy's followers.

If true lovers have always been thwarted, then it must be a law of fate. So let us learn to be patient in our trouble, because it is a normal part of love, as much a part of it as thoughts and dreams and sighs, wishes and tears, the usual companions of love.

A good persuasion; therefore, hear me, Hermia. / I have a widow aunt, a dowager / Of great revenue, and she hath no child. / From Athens is her house remote seven leagues, / And she respects me as her only son. / There, gentle Hermia, may I marry thee, / And to that place the sharp Athenian law / Cannot pursue us. If thou lovest me then, / Steal forth thy father's house tomorrow night; / And in the wood, a league without the town / (Where I did meet thee once with Helena / To do observance to a morn of May), / There will I stay for thee.

That is the right attitude. So listen to me, Hermia. I have an aunt, a rich widow with no children. Her house is twenty miles from Athens, and she treats me like her own son. There, sweet Hermia, I can marry you, and the harsh Athenian law cannot follow us there. So, if you love me, slip out of your father's house tomorrow night. In the wood three miles outside the town, where I once met you with Helena to celebrate a May morning, I will wait for you.

My good Lysander! / I swear to thee by Cupid's strongest bow, / By his best arrow with the golden head, / By the simplicity of Venus' doves, / By that which knitteth souls and prospers loves, / And by that fire which burn'd the Carthage queen / When the false Trojan under sail was seen, / By all the vows that ever men have broke / (In number more than ever women spoke), / In that same place thou hast appointed me, / Tomorrow truly will I meet with thee.

My dear Lysander! I swear to you by Cupid's strongest bow, by his best arrow with the golden tip, by the innocence of Venus's doves, by everything that binds souls together and makes love grow, by the fire that burned Dido, the Queen of Carthage, when she saw her lover Aeneas sail away, and by every promise men have ever broken (more promises than women have ever made): tomorrow I will meet you without fail in the place you have chosen.
Keep promise, love. Look, here comes Helena.
Keep your promise, my love. Look, here comes Helena.
God speed fair Helena! Whither away?
Hello, beautiful Helena! Where are you going?

Call you me fair? That fair again unsay. / Demetrius loves your fair. O happy fair! / Your eyes are lode-stars and your tongue's sweet air / More tuneable than lark to shepherd's ear, / When wheat is green, when hawthorn buds appear. / Sickness is catching. O were favour so, / Yours would I catch, fair Hermia, ere I go. / My ear should catch your voice, my eye your eye, / My tongue should catch your tongue's sweet melody. / Were the world mine, Demetrius being bated, / The rest I'd give to be to you translated. / O, teach me how you look, and with what art / You sway the motion of Demetrius' heart!

Did you call me beautiful? Take that back. Demetrius loves your beauty. Lucky beauty! Your eyes are guiding stars, and your sweet voice is more musical than a lark's song is to a shepherd in spring, when the wheat is green and the hawthorn comes into bud. Illness is catching. If only good looks were catching too! I would catch yours, beautiful Hermia, before I left. My ear would catch your voice, my eye your eye, my tongue your sweet way of speaking. If the world were mine, I'd give it all, except Demetrius, to be changed into you. Oh, teach me how you look at him, and what trick you use to control Demetrius's heart!
I frown upon him, yet he loves me still.
I frown at him, but he still loves me.
O that your frowns would teach my smiles such skill!
If only my smiles could learn to work as well as your frowns!
I give him curses, yet he gives me love.
I curse him, but he gives me love.
O that my prayers could such affection move!
If only my prayers could make him feel that way!
The more I hate, the more he follows me.
The more I hate him, the more he follows me.
The more I love, the more he hateth me.
The more I love him, the more he hates me.
His folly, Helena, is no fault of mine.
His foolishness isn't my fault, Helena.
None but your beauty; would that fault were mine!
No, it's your beauty's fault. I wish I had that fault!

Take comfort: he no more shall see my face; / Lysander and myself will fly this place. / Before the time I did Lysander see, / Seem'd Athens as a paradise to me. / O, then, what graces in my love do dwell, / That he hath turn'd a heaven into hell!

Cheer up. He won't see my face again. Lysander and I are going to run away from here. Before I met Lysander, Athens seemed like paradise to me. So what powers my love must have, to turn heaven into hell!

Helen, to you our minds we will unfold: / Tomorrow night, when Phoebe doth behold / Her silver visage in the watery glass, / Decking with liquid pearl the bladed grass / (A time that lovers' flights doth still conceal), / Through Athens' gates have we devis'd to steal.

Helena, we'll tell you our plans. Tomorrow night, when the moon sees her silver face reflected in the water and decorates the blades of grass with drops of dew like pearls (a time that always hides lovers who run away), we plan to slip out through the gates of Athens.

And in the wood where often you and I / Upon faint primrose beds were wont to lie, / Emptying our bosoms of their counsel sweet, / There my Lysander and myself shall meet, / And thence from Athens turn away our eyes, / To seek new friends and stranger companies. / Farewell, sweet playfellow. Pray thou for us, / And good luck grant thee thy Demetrius! / Keep word, Lysander. We must starve our sight / From lovers' food, till morrow deep midnight.

And in the wood, where you and I used to lie on beds of pale primroses telling each other our sweet secrets, Lysander and I will meet. From there we will turn our backs on Athens and look for new friends among strangers. Goodbye, sweet friend of my childhood. Pray for us, and good luck in winning your Demetrius! Keep your word, Lysander. We must starve our eyes of the sight of each other, which is lovers' food, until midnight tomorrow.
Helena, adieu. / As you on him, Demetrius dote on you!
Goodbye, Helena. I hope Demetrius comes to love you as much as you love him!

How happy some o'er other some can be! / Through Athens I am thought as fair as she. / But what of that? Demetrius thinks not so; / He will not know what all but he do know. / And as he errs, doting on Hermia's eyes, / So I, admiring of his qualities. / Things base and vile, holding no quantity, / Love can transpose to form and dignity. / Love looks not with the eyes, but with the mind; / And therefore is wing'd Cupid painted blind. / Nor hath love's mind of any judgment taste. / Wings, and no eyes, figure unheedy haste. / And therefore is love said to be a child, / Because in choice he is so oft beguil'd. / As waggish boys in game themselves forswear, / So the boy Love is perjur'd everywhere. / For, ere Demetrius look'd on Hermia's eyne, / He hail'd down oaths that he was only mine; / And when this hail some heat from Hermia felt, / So he dissolv'd, and showers of oaths did melt. / I will go tell him of fair Hermia's flight. / Then to the wood will he tomorrow night / Pursue her; and for this intelligence / If I have thanks, it is a dear expense. / But herein mean I to enrich my pain, / To have his sight thither and back again.

How much happier some people are than others! All over Athens I'm thought to be as beautiful as she is. But so what? Demetrius doesn't think so. He refuses to see what everyone except him can see. And just as he is wrong to be obsessed with Hermia's eyes, so am I wrong to admire everything about him. Love can turn things that are low and worthless into something fine and dignified. Love doesn't see with the eyes but with the mind, and that is why winged Cupid is painted blind. Love's mind has no judgement at all: wings and no eyes stand for reckless hurry. That's why Love is said to be a child: because he is so often fooled in his choices. Just as naughty boys break their promises in games, so the boy Love tells lies everywhere. Before Demetrius saw Hermia's eyes, he showered me with promises that he was mine alone. But when that hail of promises felt some heat from Hermia, he melted, and his promises melted away too. I will go and tell him that Hermia is running away. Then tomorrow night he will follow her to the wood. If he thanks me for this news, it will cost me dearly. But I mean to make my pain worth it by seeing him on the way there and back again.
You were best to call them generally, man by man, according to the / scrip.
You'd better call them all one by one, man by man, from the list.
Here is the scroll of every man's name, which is thought fit through / all Athens, to play in our interlude before the Duke and Duchess, on / his wedding-day at night.
Here's the list of names of every man in Athens who is thought good enough to act in our play before the Duke and Duchess on the night of his wedding.
First, good Peter Quince, say what the play treats on; then read the / names of the actors; and so grow to a point.
First, good Peter Quince, tell us what the play is about, then read out the actors' names, and so get to the point.
Marry, our play is The most lamentable comedy and most cruel death of / Pyramus and Thisbe.
Well, our play is The Most Sad Comedy and Most Cruel Death of Pyramus and Thisbe.
A very good piece of work, I assure you, and a merry. Now, good Peter / Quince, call forth your actors by the scroll. Masters, spread / yourselves.
A very good piece of work, I promise you, and a cheerful one. Now, good Peter Quince, call out your actors from the list. Gentlemen, spread out.
Answer, as I call you. Nick Bottom, the weaver.
Answer when I call your name. Nick Bottom, the weaver.
Ready. Name what part I am for, and proceed.
Here. Tell me which part I'm playing, and carry on.
You, Nick Bottom, are set down for Pyramus.
You, Nick Bottom, are down to play Pyramus.
What is Pyramus—a lover, or a tyrant?
What is Pyramus? A lover or a tyrant?
A lover, that kills himself most gallantly for love.
A lover, who kills himself very bravely for love.

That will ask some tears in the true performing of it. If I do it, let / the audience look to their eyes. I will move storms; I will condole in / some measure. To the rest—yet my chief humour is for a tyrant. I could / play Ercles rarely, or a part to tear a cat in, to make all split. / The raging rocks / And shivering shocks / Shall break the locks / Of prison gates, / And Phibbus' car / Shall shine from far, / And make and mar / The foolish Fates. / This was lofty. Now name the rest of the players. This is Ercles' vein, / a tyrant's vein; a lover is more condoling.

That will need some tears to do it properly. If I play it, the audience had better watch out for their eyes. I'll whip up storms of weeping; I'll lament in style. Now the rest. But what I'm really best at is a tyrant. I could play Hercules wonderfully, or a part where I rant and rave and bring the house down. 'The raging rocks and shivering shocks shall break the locks of prison gates, and Phoebus's chariot shall shine from far, and make and mar the foolish Fates.' That was magnificent! Now name the rest of the actors. That's the Hercules style, the tyrant style. A lover is more full of sorrow.
Flute, you must take Thisbe on you.
Flute, you must take on Thisbe.
What is Thisbe? A wandering knight?
Who is Thisbe? A knight on a quest?
It is the lady that Pyramus must love.
She's the lady Pyramus has to love.
Nay, faith, let not me play a woman. I have a beard coming.
No, honestly, don't make me play a woman. My beard is starting to grow.
That's all one. You shall play it in a mask, and you may speak as small / as you will.
That doesn't matter. You'll wear a mask, and you can speak in as high a voice as you like.
And I may hide my face, let me play Thisbe too. I'll speak in a / monstrous little voice; 'Thisne, Thisne!'—'Ah, Pyramus, my lover dear! / thy Thisbe dear! and lady dear!'
If I can hide my face, let me play Thisbe too. I'll speak in an amazingly tiny voice: 'Thisne, Thisne!' 'Ah, Pyramus, my dear lover! Your dear Thisbe, your dear lady!'
No, no, you must play Pyramus; and, Flute, you Thisbe.
No, no, you must play Pyramus; and Flute, you play Thisbe.
Robin Starveling, you must play Thisbe's mother. / Tom Snout, the tinker.
Robin Starveling, you must play Thisbe's mother. Tom Snout, the tinker.
You, Pyramus' father; myself, Thisbe's father; / Snug, the joiner, you, the lion's part. And, I hope here is a play / fitted.
You'll play Pyramus's father. I'll be Thisbe's father. Snug, the joiner, you have the lion's part. And there, I hope, we have a well-cast play.
Have you the lion's part written? Pray you, if it be, give it me, for I / am slow of study.
Have you got the lion's part written out? If you have, please give it to me, because I'm slow at learning lines.
You may do it extempore, for it is nothing but roaring.
You can make it up as you go along, because it's nothing but roaring.
Let me play the lion too. I will roar that I will do any man's heart / good to hear me. I will roar that I will make the Duke say 'Let him / roar again, let him roar again.'
Let me play the lion too. I'll roar so well that it will do everyone's heart good to hear me. I'll roar so well that the Duke will say, 'Let him roar again, let him roar again!'
If you should do it too terribly, you would fright the Duchess and the / ladies, that they would shriek; and that were enough to hang us all.
If you did it too fiercely, you'd frighten the Duchess and the ladies so much that they'd scream, and that would be enough to get us all hanged.
That would hang us every mother's son.
That would get every one of us hanged.

I grant you, friends, if you should fright the ladies out of their / wits, they would have no more discretion but to hang us. But I will / aggravate my voice so, that I will roar you as gently as any sucking / dove; I will roar you an 'twere any nightingale.

I agree, friends, that if you frightened the ladies out of their minds, they'd have no choice but to hang us. But I'll 'aggravate' my voice so that I roar as gently as a baby dove. I'll roar for you as sweetly as a nightingale.
You can play no part but Pyramus, for Pyramus is a sweet-faced man; a / proper man as one shall see in a summer's day; a most lovely / gentleman-like man. Therefore you must needs play Pyramus.
You can't play any part except Pyramus, because Pyramus is a sweet-faced man, as handsome a man as you'll see on a summer's day, a most lovely, gentlemanly man. So you simply have to play Pyramus.
Well, I will undertake it. What beard were I best to play it in?
Well, I'll take it on. What beard would be best to play it in?
I will discharge it in either your straw-colour beard, your / orange-tawny beard, your purple-in-grain beard, or your / French-crown-colour beard, your perfect yellow.
I'll perform it in either the straw-coloured beard, the orange-brown beard, the deep purple beard, or the beard the colour of a French gold coin, a perfect yellow.

Some of your French crowns have no hair at all, and then you will play / bare-faced. But, masters, here are your parts, and I am to entreat you, / request you, and desire you, to con them by tomorrow night; and meet me / in the palace wood, a mile without the town, by moonlight; there will / we rehearse, for if we meet in the city, we shall be dogg'd with / company, and our devices known. In the meantime I will draw a bill of / properties, such as our play wants. I pray you fail me not.

Some French heads have no hair at all, so then you'd be playing bare-faced. But, gentlemen, here are your parts, and I beg you, ask you and want you to learn them by tomorrow night. Meet me in the palace wood, a mile outside the town, by moonlight. We'll rehearse there, because if we meet in the city we'll be followed by crowds and our plans will be found out. Meanwhile I'll make a list of the props our play needs. Please don't let me down.
We will meet, and there we may rehearse most obscenely and / courageously. Take pains, be perfect; adieu.
We'll meet, and there we can rehearse 'obscenely' and bravely. Work hard, know your lines perfectly. Goodbye.
At the Duke's oak we meet.
We'll meet at the Duke's oak.
That's settled. Be there, or else.
How now, spirit! Whither wander you?
Hello there, spirit! Where are you off to?

Over hill, over dale, / Thorough bush, thorough brier, / Over park, over pale, / Thorough flood, thorough fire, / I do wander everywhere, / Swifter than the moon's sphere; / And I serve the Fairy Queen, / To dew her orbs upon the green. / The cowslips tall her pensioners be, / In their gold coats spots you see; / Those be rubies, fairy favours, / In those freckles live their savours. / I must go seek some dew-drops here, / And hang a pearl in every cowslip's ear. / Farewell, thou lob of spirits; I'll be gone. / Our Queen and all her elves come here anon.

Over hills, over valleys, through bushes, through briars, over parks, over fences, through floods, through fire, I wander everywhere, faster than the moon moves in its orbit. I serve the Fairy Queen and sprinkle dew on her fairy rings in the grass. The tall cowslips are her bodyguards. You can see spots on their golden coats: those are rubies, gifts from the fairies, and their sweet scent lives in those freckles. I have to go and find some dewdrops here and hang a pearl in every cowslip's ear. Goodbye, you clumsy lump of a spirit. I'll be off. Our Queen and all her elves will be here any minute.

The King doth keep his revels here tonight; / Take heed the Queen come not within his sight, / For Oberon is passing fell and wrath, / Because that she, as her attendant, hath / A lovely boy, stol'n from an Indian king; / She never had so sweet a changeling. / And jealous Oberon would have the child / Knight of his train, to trace the forests wild: / But she perforce withholds the lovèd boy, / Crowns him with flowers, and makes him all her joy. / And now they never meet in grove or green, / By fountain clear, or spangled starlight sheen, / But they do square; that all their elves for fear / Creep into acorn cups, and hide them there.

The King is holding his party here tonight. Make sure the Queen doesn't come anywhere near him, because Oberon is extremely angry. She has a lovely boy as her servant, stolen from an Indian king; she never had such a sweet stolen child. Jealous Oberon wants the boy to be a knight in his own following, to roam the wild forests. But she refuses to give up the boy she loves, crowns him with flowers and makes him her whole delight. Now whenever they meet, in a wood or a meadow, by a clear spring or under the shining stars, they quarrel, so that all their elves crawl into acorn cups in fear and hide there.

Either I mistake your shape and making quite, / Or else you are that shrewd and knavish sprite / Call'd Robin Goodfellow. Are not you he / That frights the maidens of the villagery, / Skim milk, and sometimes labour in the quern, / And bootless make the breathless housewife churn, / And sometime make the drink to bear no barm, / Mislead night-wanderers, laughing at their harm? / Those that Hobgoblin call you, and sweet Puck, / You do their work, and they shall have good luck. / Are not you he?

Either I've got your looks completely wrong, or you are that cunning, mischievous spirit called Robin Goodfellow. Aren't you the one who scares the village girls, skims the cream off the milk, sometimes works the hand-mill so the flour comes out wrong, and makes the housewife churn till she's out of breath with no butter to show for it? Who sometimes stops the beer from frothing, and leads night travellers the wrong way, laughing at their trouble? Those who call you Hobgoblin and sweet Puck, you do their work for them, and they have good luck. Aren't you him?

Thou speak'st aright; / I am that merry wanderer of the night. / I jest to Oberon, and make him smile, / When I a fat and bean-fed horse beguile, / Neighing in likeness of a filly foal; / And sometime lurk I in a gossip's bowl / In very likeness of a roasted crab, / And, when she drinks, against her lips I bob, / And on her withered dewlap pour the ale. / The wisest aunt, telling the saddest tale, / Sometime for three-foot stool mistaketh me; / Then slip I from her bum, down topples she, / And 'tailor' cries, and falls into a cough; / And then the whole quire hold their hips and loffe / And waxen in their mirth, and neeze, and swear / A merrier hour was never wasted there. / But room, fairy. Here comes Oberon.

You've got it right. I am that cheerful night wanderer. I tell jokes to Oberon and make him smile, when I trick a fat, well-fed stallion by neighing like a young female horse. Sometimes I hide in an old woman's drink, looking exactly like a roasted crab apple, and when she drinks I bob against her lips and make her spill the ale down her wrinkled neck. The wisest old aunt, telling the saddest story, sometimes mistakes me for a three-legged stool. Then I slip out from under her bum, down she tumbles, shouts 'Ouch, my backside!' and starts coughing. Then the whole group hold their sides and laugh, and get merrier, and sneeze, and swear they never had a better time. But make way, fairy. Here comes Oberon.
And here my mistress. Would that he were gone!
And here comes my mistress. I wish he would go away!
Ill met by moonlight, proud Titania.
An unlucky meeting by moonlight, proud Titania.
What, jealous Oberon! Fairies, skip hence; / I have forsworn his bed and company.
What, jealous Oberon! Fairies, let's go. I have sworn to stay out of his bed and his company.
Tarry, rash wanton; am not I thy lord?
Wait, you headstrong, unfaithful woman! Aren't I your husband?

Then I must be thy lady; but I know / When thou hast stol'n away from fairyland, / And in the shape of Corin sat all day / Playing on pipes of corn, and versing love / To amorous Phillida. Why art thou here, / Come from the farthest steep of India, / But that, forsooth, the bouncing Amazon, / Your buskin'd mistress and your warrior love, / To Theseus must be wedded; and you come / To give their bed joy and prosperity?

Then I must be your wife. But I know about the times you've sneaked off from fairyland, and sat all day disguised as the shepherd Corin, playing on straw pipes and reciting love poems to the lovesick shepherdess Phillida. Why have you come here, all the way from the furthest mountains of India? It's only because, of course, that strapping Amazon, your mistress in her hunting boots, your warrior love, is going to marry Theseus, and you've come to bless their marriage bed with joy and good fortune.

How canst thou thus, for shame, Titania, / Glance at my credit with Hippolyta, / Knowing I know thy love to Theseus? / Didst not thou lead him through the glimmering night / From Perigenia, whom he ravished? / And make him with fair Aegles break his faith, / With Ariadne and Antiopa?

How can you, shameless Titania, hint at my friendship with Hippolyta, when you know I know about your love for Theseus? Didn't you lead him through the starlit night away from Perigenia, whom he had raped? And make him break his promises to beautiful Aegles, to Ariadne and to Antiopa?

These are the forgeries of jealousy: / And never, since the middle summer's spring, / Met we on hill, in dale, forest, or mead, / By pavèd fountain, or by rushy brook, / Or on the beachèd margent of the sea, / To dance our ringlets to the whistling wind, / But with thy brawls thou hast disturb'd our sport. / Therefore the winds, piping to us in vain, / As in revenge, have suck'd up from the sea / Contagious fogs; which, falling in the land, / Hath every pelting river made so proud / That they have overborne their continents. / The ox hath therefore stretch'd his yoke in vain, / The ploughman lost his sweat, and the green corn / Hath rotted ere his youth attain'd a beard. / The fold stands empty in the drownèd field, / And crows are fatted with the murrion flock; / The nine-men's-morris is fill'd up with mud, / And the quaint mazes in the wanton green, / For lack of tread, are undistinguishable. / The human mortals want their winter here. / No night is now with hymn or carol blest. / Therefore the moon, the governess of floods, / Pale in her anger, washes all the air, / That rheumatic diseases do abound. / And thorough this distemperature we see / The seasons alter: hoary-headed frosts / Fall in the fresh lap of the crimson rose; / And on old Hiems' thin and icy crown / An odorous chaplet of sweet summer buds / Is, as in mockery, set. The spring, the summer, / The childing autumn, angry winter, change / Their wonted liveries; and the mazed world, / By their increase, now knows not which is which. / And this same progeny of evils comes / From our debate, from our dissension; / We are their parents and original.

These are lies made up by jealousy. Ever since the start of midsummer, we have never met on a hill, in a valley, forest or meadow, by a stone-lined spring or a reedy stream, or on the sandy edge of the sea, to dance our circles to the whistling wind, without you spoiling our fun with your quarrelling. So the winds, piping to us for nothing, have taken revenge by sucking up poisonous fogs from the sea. These have fallen on the land and made every little river so swollen that they have burst their banks. So the ox has pulled his plough for nothing, the ploughman has wasted his sweat, and the green corn has rotted before it could ripen. The sheep pens stand empty in the flooded fields, and crows grow fat on the dead, diseased flocks. The outdoor game boards are filled with mud, and the intricate paths in the lush grass can't be seen, because no one walks on them. The humans are missing their winter festivities. No night is blessed with hymns or carols now. So the moon, which rules the tides, pale with anger, soaks the air with damp, and colds and fevers are everywhere. Because of this disorder, the seasons are changing. White frosts fall on the fresh red rose, and on old Winter's thin, icy head a sweet-smelling crown of summer buds is placed, as if to mock him. Spring, summer, fruitful autumn and angry winter swap their usual clothes, and the confused world can't tell which is which from what they produce. And this whole family of disasters comes from our argument, our quarrel. We are their parents and their origin.
Do you amend it, then. It lies in you. / Why should Titania cross her Oberon? / I do but beg a little changeling boy / To be my henchman.
Then you put it right. It's in your power. Why should Titania go against her Oberon? All I'm asking for is a little stolen boy to be my page.

Set your heart at rest; / The fairyland buys not the child of me. / His mother was a vot'ress of my order, / And in the spicèd Indian air, by night, / Full often hath she gossip'd by my side; / And sat with me on Neptune's yellow sands, / Marking th' embarkèd traders on the flood, / When we have laugh'd to see the sails conceive, / And grow big-bellied with the wanton wind; / Which she, with pretty and with swimming gait / Following (her womb then rich with my young squire), / Would imitate, and sail upon the land, / To fetch me trifles, and return again, / As from a voyage, rich with merchandise. / But she, being mortal, of that boy did die; / And for her sake do I rear up her boy, / And for her sake I will not part with him.

Forget it. You couldn't buy the child from me with all of fairyland. His mother was a follower of mine, and on many nights in the spicy Indian air she sat chatting beside me, and sat with me on the yellow sands by the sea, watching the merchant ships on the waves. We laughed to see the sails swell up as if they were pregnant, puffed out by the playful wind. She would copy them, walking with a pretty, swaying step (her womb was carrying my young page then), and sail across the land to fetch me little presents, and come back as if from a voyage, loaded with goods. But she was mortal, and she died giving birth to that boy. For her sake I am bringing up her son, and for her sake I won't give him up.
How long within this wood intend you stay?
How long do you plan to stay in this wood?
Perchance till after Theseus' wedding-day. / If you will patiently dance in our round, / And see our moonlight revels, go with us; / If not, shun me, and I will spare your haunts.
Maybe until after Theseus's wedding day. If you will dance calmly in our circle and watch our moonlit celebrations, come with us. If not, keep away from me, and I'll stay away from the places you go.
Give me that boy and I will go with thee.
Give me that boy and I'll come with you.
Not for thy fairy kingdom. Fairies, away. / We shall chide downright if I longer stay.
Not for your whole fairy kingdom. Fairies, let's go. We'll have a real fight if I stay any longer.

Well, go thy way. Thou shalt not from this grove / Till I torment thee for this injury.— / My gentle Puck, come hither. Thou rememb'rest / Since once I sat upon a promontory, / And heard a mermaid on a dolphin's back / Uttering such dulcet and harmonious breath / That the rude sea grew civil at her song / And certain stars shot madly from their spheres / To hear the sea-maid's music.

All right, go your way. You won't leave this wood until I've punished you for this insult. My gentle Puck, come here. Do you remember when I sat on a headland and heard a mermaid on a dolphin's back singing so sweetly and harmoniously that the rough sea grew calm at her song, and some stars shot wildly out of their orbits to hear the sea-girl's music?

That very time I saw, (but thou couldst not), / Flying between the cold moon and the earth, / Cupid all arm'd: a certain aim he took / At a fair vestal, thronèd by the west, / And loos'd his love-shaft smartly from his bow / As it should pierce a hundred thousand hearts. / But I might see young Cupid's fiery shaft / Quench'd in the chaste beams of the watery moon; / And the imperial votress passed on, / In maiden meditation, fancy-free. / Yet mark'd I where the bolt of Cupid fell: / It fell upon a little western flower, / Before milk-white, now purple with love's wound, / And maidens call it love-in-idleness. / Fetch me that flower, the herb I showed thee once: / The juice of it on sleeping eyelids laid / Will make or man or woman madly dote / Upon the next live creature that it sees. / Fetch me this herb, and be thou here again / Ere the leviathan can swim a league.

At that very moment I saw (though you couldn't) Cupid, fully armed, flying between the cold moon and the earth. He took careful aim at a beautiful virgin queen, enthroned in the west, and shot his love-arrow sharply from his bow, as if it could pierce a hundred thousand hearts. But I saw young Cupid's fiery arrow put out by the pure rays of the watery moon, and the royal virgin walked on, lost in innocent thoughts, free of love. But I noticed where Cupid's arrow fell. It fell on a little western flower, which used to be milk-white but is now purple from love's wound. Girls call it love-in-idleness. Fetch me that flower, the herb I once showed you. Its juice, put on sleeping eyelids, will make a man or woman fall madly in love with the next living creature they see. Fetch me this herb, and be back before a whale can swim three miles.
I'll put a girdle round about the earth / In forty minutes.
I'll fly a belt around the whole earth in forty minutes.

Having once this juice, / I'll watch Titania when she is asleep, / And drop the liquor of it in her eyes: / The next thing then she waking looks upon / (Be it on lion, bear, or wolf, or bull, / On meddling monkey, or on busy ape) / She shall pursue it with the soul of love. / And ere I take this charm from off her sight / (As I can take it with another herb) / I'll make her render up her page to me. / But who comes here? I am invisible; / And I will overhear their conference.

Once I have this juice, I'll watch Titania until she is asleep and drop the liquid in her eyes. The next thing she sees when she wakes up, whether it's a lion, a bear, a wolf or a bull, an interfering monkey or a busy ape, she will chase it with all her soul in love. And before I take this spell off her eyes (which I can do with another herb), I'll make her hand over her page to me. But who's coming? I am invisible, and I'll listen to their conversation.

I love thee not, therefore pursue me not. / Where is Lysander and fair Hermia? / The one I'll slay, the other slayeth me. / Thou told'st me they were stol'n into this wood, / And here am I, and wode within this wood / Because I cannot meet with Hermia. / Hence, get thee gone, and follow me no more.

I don't love you, so stop following me. Where are Lysander and beautiful Hermia? I'll kill the one, and the other is killing me. You told me they had slipped away into this wood, and here I am, going wild in this wood because I can't find Hermia. Go away, get out, and stop following me.
You draw me, you hard-hearted adamant, / But yet you draw not iron, for my heart / Is true as steel. Leave you your power to draw, / And I shall have no power to follow you.
You pull me to you, you hard-hearted magnet. But it isn't iron you attract, because my heart is as true as steel. Give up your power to attract me, and I'll have no power to follow you.
Do I entice you? Do I speak you fair? / Or rather do I not in plainest truth / Tell you I do not, nor I cannot love you?
Do I lead you on? Do I speak kindly to you? Don't I tell you, as plainly as I can, that I don't love you and can't love you?

And even for that do I love you the more. / I am your spaniel; and, Demetrius, / The more you beat me, I will fawn on you. / Use me but as your spaniel, spurn me, strike me, / Neglect me, lose me; only give me leave, / Unworthy as I am, to follow you. / What worser place can I beg in your love, / (And yet a place of high respect with me) / Than to be usèd as you use your dog?

And that's exactly why I love you more. I am your spaniel, and, Demetrius, the more you beat me, the more I'll fawn over you. Just treat me as your spaniel: kick me, hit me, ignore me, lose me. Only let me follow you, unworthy as I am. What lower place could I ask for in your love (and yet to me it's a place of great honour) than to be treated the way you treat your dog?
Tempt not too much the hatred of my spirit; / For I am sick when I do look on thee.
Don't push my hatred too far. It makes me sick to look at you.
And I am sick when I look not on you.
And I am sick when I can't look at you.

You do impeach your modesty too much / To leave the city and commit yourself / Into the hands of one that loves you not, / To trust the opportunity of night / And the ill counsel of a desert place, / With the rich worth of your virginity.

You are putting your reputation at great risk by leaving the city and handing yourself over to a man who doesn't love you, trusting your precious virginity to the chances of the night and the temptations of a lonely place.

Your virtue is my privilege: for that / It is not night when I do see your face, / Therefore I think I am not in the night; / Nor doth this wood lack worlds of company, / For you, in my respect, are all the world. / Then how can it be said I am alone / When all the world is here to look on me?

Your good character is my protection. And because it is never night when I see your face, I don't feel I'm in the dark. Nor is this wood short of company, because to me you are the whole world. So how can anyone say I'm alone, when the whole world is here looking at me?
I'll run from thee and hide me in the brakes, / And leave thee to the mercy of wild beasts.
I'll run away from you and hide in the bushes, and leave you to the mercy of wild animals.

The wildest hath not such a heart as you. / Run when you will, the story shall be chang'd; / Apollo flies, and Daphne holds the chase; / The dove pursues the griffin, the mild hind / Makes speed to catch the tiger. Bootless speed, / When cowardice pursues and valour flies!

The wildest animal doesn't have a heart as cruel as yours. Run whenever you like; the old story will be turned round. Apollo will run away and Daphne will chase him. The dove will chase the griffin, the gentle deer will hurry to catch the tiger. But speeding is useless when the coward chases and the brave one runs away!
I will not stay thy questions. Let me go, / Or if thou follow me, do not believe / But I shall do thee mischief in the wood.
I won't stay to listen to you. Let me go. Or if you follow me, you can be sure I'll do you some harm in the wood.

Ay, in the temple, in the town, the field, / You do me mischief. Fie, Demetrius! / Your wrongs do set a scandal on my sex. / We cannot fight for love as men may do. / We should be woo'd, and were not made to woo.

Yes, in the temple, in the town, in the fields, you do me harm. Shame on you, Demetrius! The wrongs you do me make my whole sex look disgraceful. We women can't fight for love the way men can. We are supposed to be courted, not to do the courting.
I'll follow thee, and make a heaven of hell, / To die upon the hand I love so well.
I'll follow you and turn this hell into heaven, if I can die by the hand of the man I love so much.
Fare thee well, nymph. Ere he do leave this grove, / Thou shalt fly him, and he shall seek thy love.
Goodbye, nymph. Before he leaves this wood, you will be the one running away, and he will be chasing your love.
Hast thou the flower there? Welcome, wanderer.
Have you got the flower? Welcome, wanderer.

I pray thee give it me. / I know a bank where the wild thyme blows, / Where oxlips and the nodding violet grows, / Quite over-canopied with luscious woodbine, / With sweet musk-roses, and with eglantine. / There sleeps Titania sometime of the night, / Lull'd in these flowers with dances and delight; / And there the snake throws her enamell'd skin, / Weed wide enough to wrap a fairy in. / And with the juice of this I'll streak her eyes, / And make her full of hateful fantasies. / Take thou some of it, and seek through this grove: / A sweet Athenian lady is in love / With a disdainful youth. Anoint his eyes; / But do it when the next thing he espies / May be the lady. Thou shalt know the man / By the Athenian garments he hath on. / Effect it with some care, that he may prove / More fond on her than she upon her love: / And look thou meet me ere the first cock crow.

Please give it to me. I know a bank where wild thyme blooms, where oxlips and nodding violets grow, all roofed over with rich honeysuckle, sweet musk roses and wild roses. Titania sleeps there for part of the night, lulled to sleep among these flowers by dancing and pleasure. There the snake sheds its shiny skin, a garment wide enough to wrap a fairy in. I'll smear her eyes with the juice of this flower and fill her head with horrible fantasies. Take some of it and search through this wood. A sweet Athenian lady is in love with a young man who scorns her. Put some on his eyes, but do it when the next thing he sees will be the lady. You'll recognise the man by his Athenian clothes. Do it carefully, so that he ends up more in love with her than she is with him. And make sure you meet me before the first cock crows.
Fear not, my lord, your servant shall do so.
Don't worry, my lord. Your servant will do it.

Come, now a roundel and a fairy song; / Then for the third part of a minute, hence; / Some to kill cankers in the musk-rose buds; / Some war with reremice for their leathern wings, / To make my small elves coats; and some keep back / The clamorous owl, that nightly hoots and wonders / At our quaint spirits. Sing me now asleep; / Then to your offices, and let me rest. / [Fairies sing]

Come on, now, a dance in a ring and a fairy song. Then, for a third of a minute, off you go. Some of you, kill the grubs in the musk-rose buds. Some of you, fight the bats for their leathery wings, to make coats for my little elves. And some of you, keep away the noisy owl that hoots all night, amazed at our dainty spirits. Now sing me to sleep. Then off to your jobs, and let me rest. [The fairies sing]
You spotted snakes with double tongue, / Thorny hedgehogs, be not seen; / Newts and blind-worms do no wrong, / Come not near our Fairy Queen:
You spotted snakes with forked tongues, prickly hedgehogs, keep out of sight. Newts and slow-worms, do no harm. Don't come near our Fairy Queen.
Philomel, with melody, / Sing in our sweet lullaby: / Lulla, lulla, lullaby; lulla, lulla, lullaby. / Never harm, nor spell, nor charm, / Come our lovely lady nigh; / So good night, with lullaby.
Nightingale, sing with your melody in our sweet lullaby: lulla, lulla, lullaby; lulla, lulla, lullaby. Let no harm, no spell and no charm come near our lovely lady. So good night, with a lullaby.
Weaving spiders, come not here; / Hence, you long-legg'd spinners, hence. / Beetles black, approach not near; / Worm nor snail do no offence.
Weaving spiders, don't come here. Away with you, long-legged spinners, away! Black beetles, don't come near. Worms and snails, do no harm.
Nightingale, with melody, and so on.
Hence away! Now all is well. / One aloof stand sentinel.
Away now! All is well. One of you stay at a distance and keep guard.
What thou seest when thou dost wake,
Whatever you see when you wake,

Do it for thy true love take; / Love and languish for his sake. / Be it ounce, or cat, or bear, / Pard, or boar with bristled hair, / In thy eye that shall appear / When thou wak'st, it is thy dear. / Wake when some vile thing is near.

take it to be your true love. Love it and long for it. Whether it's a lynx, or a cat, or a bear, a leopard or a boar with bristly hair, whatever appears before your eyes when you wake will be your darling. Wake up when some horrible thing is near.
Fair love, you faint with wand'ring in the wood. / And, to speak troth, I have forgot our way. / We'll rest us, Hermia, if you think it good, / And tarry for the comfort of the day.
My lovely one, you're exhausted from wandering in the wood. And to tell you the truth, I've lost our way. We'll rest, Hermia, if you think it's a good idea, and wait for daylight to help us.
Be it so, Lysander: find you out a bed, / For I upon this bank will rest my head.
All right, Lysander. Find yourself a bed, because I'm going to rest my head on this bank.
One turf shall serve as pillow for us both; / One heart, one bed, two bosoms, and one troth.
One piece of turf will do as a pillow for us both: one heart, one bed, two bodies and one promise.
Nay, good Lysander; for my sake, my dear, / Lie further off yet, do not lie so near.
No, good Lysander. For my sake, my dear, lie further away. Don't lie so close.

O take the sense, sweet, of my innocence! / Love takes the meaning in love's conference. / I mean that my heart unto yours is knit, / So that but one heart we can make of it: / Two bosoms interchainèd with an oath, / So then two bosoms and a single troth. / Then by your side no bed-room me deny; / For lying so, Hermia, I do not lie.

Oh, sweetheart, understand that I mean nothing wrong! Lovers should understand each other's words in a loving way. I mean that my heart is so joined to yours that we can make one heart out of them. Our two hearts are chained together by a promise, so that makes two bodies and one faithful promise. So don't refuse me a place to lie beside you, because if I lie like this, Hermia, I am not lying.

Lysander riddles very prettily. / Now much beshrew my manners and my pride, / If Hermia meant to say Lysander lied! / But, gentle friend, for love and courtesy / Lie further off, in human modesty, / Such separation as may well be said / Becomes a virtuous bachelor and a maid, / So far be distant; and good night, sweet friend: / Thy love ne'er alter till thy sweet life end!

Lysander plays with words very nicely. Curse my manners and my pride if I meant to say that Lysander was lying! But, gentle friend, out of love and politeness, lie further away, as decency requires. A distance that is right for a respectable unmarried man and a young girl: keep that far away. And good night, sweet friend. May your love never change until your sweet life ends!
Amen, amen, to that fair prayer say I; / And then end life when I end loyalty! / Here is my bed. Sleep give thee all his rest!
Amen, amen to that lovely prayer, I say. And may my life end when my loyalty ends! Here is my bed. May sleep give you all its rest!
With half that wish the wisher's eyes be pressed!
May half that wish close your own eyes in rest!

Through the forest have I gone, / But Athenian found I none, / On whose eyes I might approve / This flower's force in stirring love. / Night and silence! Who is here? / Weeds of Athens he doth wear: / This is he, my master said, / Despisèd the Athenian maid; / And here the maiden, sleeping sound, / On the dank and dirty ground. / Pretty soul, she durst not lie / Near this lack-love, this kill-courtesy. / Churl, upon thy eyes I throw / All the power this charm doth owe; / When thou wak'st let love forbid / Sleep his seat on thy eyelid. / So awake when I am gone; / For I must now to Oberon.

I've been through the whole forest, but I haven't found any Athenian on whose eyes I could test this flower's power to stir up love. Night and silence! Who's this? He's wearing Athenian clothes. This is the one my master said scorned the Athenian girl. And here is the girl, fast asleep on the damp, dirty ground. Pretty thing, she didn't dare lie near this loveless, rude man. You lout, on your eyes I pour all the power this charm has. When you wake, let love keep sleep from ever settling on your eyelids again. So wake up when I've gone, because I must go back to Oberon now.
Stay, though thou kill me, sweet Demetrius.
Stop, even if you kill me, sweet Demetrius.
I charge thee, hence, and do not haunt me thus.
I order you to go away. Stop haunting me like this.
O, wilt thou darkling leave me? Do not so.
Oh, will you leave me here in the dark? Don't do that.
Stay, on thy peril; I alone will go.
Stay here, or you'll be in danger. I'm going on alone.

O, I am out of breath in this fond chase! / The more my prayer, the lesser is my grace. / Happy is Hermia, wheresoe'er she lies, / For she hath blessèd and attractive eyes. / How came her eyes so bright? Not with salt tears. / If so, my eyes are oftener wash'd than hers. / No, no, I am as ugly as a bear, / For beasts that meet me run away for fear: / Therefore no marvel though Demetrius / Do, as a monster, fly my presence thus. / What wicked and dissembling glass of mine / Made me compare with Hermia's sphery eyne? / But who is here? Lysander, on the ground! / Dead or asleep? I see no blood, no wound. / Lysander, if you live, good sir, awake.

Oh, I'm out of breath from this foolish chase! The more I beg, the less I get. Hermia is lucky, wherever she is, because she has beautiful, attractive eyes. How did her eyes become so bright? Not with salty tears. If they did, my eyes are washed more often than hers. No, no, I'm as ugly as a bear, because animals that meet me run away in fear. So it's no wonder Demetrius runs from me as if I were a monster. What lying, wicked mirror made me think I could compare with Hermia's starry eyes? But who's this? Lysander, on the ground! Dead or asleep? I can't see any blood or wound. Lysander, if you're alive, good sir, wake up.

[Waking] And run through fire I will for thy sweet sake. / Transparent Helena! Nature shows art, / That through thy bosom makes me see thy heart. / Where is Demetrius? O, how fit a word / Is that vile name to perish on my sword!

And I'd run through fire for your sweet sake! Radiant Helena! Nature works magic: I can see your heart through your breast. Where is Demetrius? Oh, how right it would be for that vile name to die on my sword!
Do not say so, Lysander, say not so. / What though he love your Hermia? Lord, what though? / Yet Hermia still loves you. Then be content.
Don't say that, Lysander, don't say it. What does it matter if he loves your Hermia? Lord, what does it matter? Hermia still loves you, so be happy.

Content with Hermia? No, I do repent / The tedious minutes I with her have spent. / Not Hermia, but Helena I love. / Who will not change a raven for a dove? / The will of man is by his reason sway'd, / And reason says you are the worthier maid. / Things growing are not ripe until their season; / So I, being young, till now ripe not to reason; / And touching now the point of human skill, / Reason becomes the marshal to my will, / And leads me to your eyes, where I o'erlook / Love's stories, written in love's richest book.

Happy with Hermia? No, I regret the boring minutes I've spent with her. It's not Hermia but Helena I love. Who wouldn't swap a raven for a dove? A man's desires are ruled by his reason, and reason says you are the better woman. Things that grow aren't ripe until their season comes, so I, being young, wasn't ripe for reason until now. Now that I've reached the peak of human judgement, reason commands my desire and leads me to your eyes, where I read love's stories, written in love's richest book.

Wherefore was I to this keen mockery born? / When at your hands did I deserve this scorn? / Is't not enough, is't not enough, young man, / That I did never, no, nor never can / Deserve a sweet look from Demetrius' eye, / But you must flout my insufficiency? / Good troth, you do me wrong, good sooth, you do, / In such disdainful manner me to woo. / But fare you well; perforce I must confess, / I thought you lord of more true gentleness. / O, that a lady of one man refus'd, / Should of another therefore be abus'd!

Why was I born to be mocked so cruelly? What have I ever done to deserve such contempt from you? Isn't it enough, isn't it enough, young man, that I never have and never can earn one kind look from Demetrius, without you making fun of how I fall short? Honestly, you do me wrong, truly you do, to court me in such a sneering way. But goodbye. I have to admit I thought you were a more genuine gentleman. Oh, that a lady rejected by one man should be insulted by another because of it!

She sees not Hermia. Hermia, sleep thou there, / And never mayst thou come Lysander near! / For, as a surfeit of the sweetest things / The deepest loathing to the stomach brings; / Or as the heresies that men do leave / Are hated most of those they did deceive; / So thou, my surfeit and my heresy, / Of all be hated, but the most of me! / And, all my powers, address your love and might / To honour Helen, and to be her knight!

She hasn't seen Hermia. Hermia, sleep there, and may you never come near Lysander again! Just as eating too many sweet things makes the stomach feel sick of them, or as men who give up false beliefs hate them most because they were fooled by them, so you, my sickness and my false belief, be hated by everyone, but most of all by me! And all my powers, use your love and strength to honour Helena and be her knight!

[Starting] Help me, Lysander, help me! Do thy best / To pluck this crawling serpent from my breast! / Ay me, for pity! What a dream was here! / Lysander, look how I do quake with fear. / Methought a serpent eat my heart away, / And you sat smiling at his cruel prey. / Lysander! What, removed? Lysander! lord! / What, out of hearing? Gone? No sound, no word? / Alack, where are you? Speak, and if you hear; / Speak, of all loves! I swoon almost with fear. / No? Then I well perceive you are not nigh. / Either death or you I'll find immediately.

Help me, Lysander, help me! Do your best to pull this crawling snake off my breast! Oh, have pity on me! What a dream that was! Lysander, look how I'm shaking with fear. I dreamed a snake was eating my heart, and you sat smiling while it attacked me. Lysander! What, gone? Lysander! My lord! What, out of earshot? Gone? No sound, no word? Oh no, where are you? Speak, if you can hear me. Speak, for love's sake! I'm almost fainting with fear. No? Then I can see you're not nearby. I'll find either you or my death straight away.

Pat, pat; and here's a marvellous convenient place for our rehearsal. / This green plot shall be our stage, this hawthorn brake our / tiring-house; and we will do it in action, as we will do it before the / Duke.

Right on time. And here's a wonderfully handy place for our rehearsal. This patch of grass will be our stage, this hawthorn bush our dressing room, and we'll act it out properly, just as we'll do it in front of the Duke.
What is it, good old Bottom?
There are things in this comedy of Pyramus and Thisbe that will never / please. First, Pyramus must draw a sword to kill himself; which the / ladies cannot abide. How answer you that?

There are things in this comedy of Pyramus and Thisbe that will never go down well. First, Pyramus has to draw a sword to kill himself, which the ladies won't be able to stand. What do you say to that?
By our Lady, that's a terrible worry.
I believe we must leave the killing out, when all is done.
I think we'll have to leave the killing out, in the end.

Not a whit; I have a device to make all well. Write me a prologue, and / let the prologue seem to say we will do no harm with our swords, and / that Pyramus is not killed indeed; and for the more better assurance, / tell them that I Pyramus am not Pyramus but Bottom the weaver. This / will put them out of fear.

Not at all. I have a plan to make everything all right. Write me a prologue, and have the prologue seem to say that we will do no harm with our swords, and that Pyramus isn't really killed. And to reassure them even more, tell them that I, Pyramus, am not Pyramus but Bottom the weaver. That will stop them being afraid.
Well, we will have such a prologue; and it shall be written in eight / and six.
All right, we'll have a prologue like that, and it will be written in lines of eight and six syllables.
No, make it two more; let it be written in eight and eight.
No, add two more. Let it be written in eight and eight.
Will not the ladies be afeard of the lion?
Won't the ladies be afraid of the lion?
I fear it, I promise you.
I'm afraid of it myself, I promise you.

Masters, you ought to consider with yourselves, to bring in (God shield / us!) a lion among ladies is a most dreadful thing. For there is not a / more fearful wild-fowl than your lion living; and we ought to look to / it.

Gentlemen, you should think carefully about this. To bring in, God help us, a lion among ladies is a most terrible thing. There's no more frightening 'wild bird' alive than your lion, and we ought to watch out.
Therefore another prologue must tell he is not a lion.
Then another prologue must tell them he isn't a lion.

Nay, you must name his name, and half his face must be seen through the / lion's neck; and he himself must speak through, saying thus, or to the / same defect: 'Ladies,' or, 'Fair ladies, I would wish you,' or, 'I / would request you,' or, 'I would entreat you, not to fear, not to / tremble: my life for yours. If you think I come hither as a lion, it / were pity of my life. No, I am no such thing; I am a man as other men / are': and there, indeed, let him name his name, and tell them plainly / he is Snug the joiner.

No, you must say his name, and half his face must show through the lion's neck, and he himself must speak through it, saying this, or something to the same 'defect': 'Ladies,' or 'Fair ladies, I would wish you,' or 'I would ask you,' or 'I would beg you, not to be afraid, not to tremble. I'd stake my life on your safety. If you think I have come here as a lion, I'd be sorry for my life. No, I am nothing of the kind. I am a man like other men.' And then, right there, let him say his name and tell them plainly that he is Snug the joiner.
Well, it shall be so. But there is two hard things: that is, to bring / the moonlight into a chamber, for you know, Pyramus and Thisbe meet by / moonlight.
All right, that's what we'll do. But there are two difficult things. One is to bring the moonlight into a room, because, you know, Pyramus and Thisbe meet by moonlight.
Doth the moon shine that night we play our play?
Does the moon shine on the night we do our play?
A calendar, a calendar! Look in the almanack; find out moonshine, find / out moonshine.
A calendar, a calendar! Look in the almanac. Find out about moonshine, find out about moonshine!
Yes, it doth shine that night.
Yes, it does shine that night.
Why, then may you leave a casement of the great chamber window, where / we play, open; and the moon may shine in at the casement.
Well then, you could leave one of the windows open in the great hall where we're performing, and the moon can shine in through the window.

Ay; or else one must come in with a bush of thorns and a lantern, and / say he comes to disfigure or to present the person of Moonshine. Then / there is another thing: we must have a wall in the great chamber; for / Pyramus and Thisbe, says the story, did talk through the chink of a / wall.

Yes, or else someone could come in with a bundle of sticks and a lantern and say he has come to 'disfigure', or to play, the character of Moonshine. Then there's another thing. We must have a wall in the great hall, because Pyramus and Thisbe, the story says, talked through a crack in a wall.
You can never bring in a wall. What say you, Bottom?
You can never bring in a wall. What do you say, Bottom?

Some man or other must present Wall. And let him have some plaster, or / some loam, or some rough-cast about him, to signify wall; and let him / hold his fingers thus, and through that cranny shall Pyramus and Thisbe / whisper.

Somebody or other must play Wall. Let him wear some plaster, or some clay, or some rough lime and gravel, to show he's a wall. And let him hold his fingers like this, and Pyramus and Thisbe can whisper through that crack.

If that may be, then all is well. Come, sit down, every mother's son, / and rehearse your parts. Pyramus, you begin: when you have spoken your / speech, enter into that brake; and so everyone according to his cue.

If we can do that, everything's fine. Come on, sit down, every one of you, and rehearse your parts. Pyramus, you start. When you've said your speech, go into that bush, and so on, everyone when it's his cue.
What hempen homespuns have we swaggering here, / So near the cradle of the Fairy Queen? / What, a play toward? I'll be an auditor; / An actor too perhaps, if I see cause.
Who are these rough peasants strutting about here, so near the Fairy Queen's bed? What, a play coming up? I'll be in the audience. Maybe an actor too, if I see a reason.
Thisbe, the flowers of odious savours sweet
Thisbe, the flowers of hateful smells are sweet...
. . . odours savours sweet. / So hath thy breath, my dearest Thisbe dear. / But hark, a voice! Stay thou but here awhile, / And by and by I will to thee appear.
...odours smell sweet. So does your breath, my dearest Thisbe dear. But listen, a voice! Wait here a while, and soon I will appear to you.
A stranger Pyramus than e'er played here!
The strangest Pyramus that's ever been played here!
Ay, marry, must you, For you must understand he goes but to see a noise / that he heard, and is to come again.
Yes, of course you do. You see, he's only gone to see about a noise he heard, and he's coming back.

Most radiant Pyramus, most lily-white of hue, / Of colour like the red rose on triumphant brier, / Most brisky juvenal, and eke most lovely Jew, / As true as truest horse, that yet would never tire, / I'll meet thee, Pyramus, at Ninny's tomb.

Most radiant Pyramus, as white as a lily, coloured like a red rose on a splendid briar, most lively youth and also most lovely 'Jew', as faithful as the most faithful horse that never gets tired, I'll meet you, Pyramus, at Ninny's tomb.
Ninus' tomb, man! Why, you must not speak that yet. That you answer to / Pyramus. You speak all your part at once, cues, and all.—Pyramus enter! / Your cue is past; it is 'never tire.'
Ninus's tomb, man! And you mustn't say that yet. That's your answer to Pyramus. You're saying your whole part at once, cues and all. Pyramus, come in! You've missed your cue. It's 'never tire'.
O, As true as truest horse, that yet would never tire.
Oh: as faithful as the most faithful horse that never gets tired.
If I were fair, Thisbe, I were only thine.
If I were handsome, Thisbe, I would be yours alone.
O monstrous! O strange! We are haunted. Pray, masters, fly, masters! / Help!
How monstrous! How strange! We're haunted! Run, gentlemen, run! Help!

I'll follow you. I'll lead you about a round, / Through bog, through bush, through brake, through brier; / Sometime a horse I'll be, sometime a hound, / A hog, a headless bear, sometime a fire; / And neigh, and bark, and grunt, and roar, and burn, / Like horse, hound, hog, bear, fire, at every turn.

I'll follow you. I'll lead you round in circles, through bog, through bush, through thicket, through briar. Sometimes I'll be a horse, sometimes a hound, a pig, a headless bear, sometimes a fire. And I'll neigh and bark and grunt and roar and burn, like a horse, hound, pig, bear and fire, at every turn.
Why do they run away? This is a knavery of them to make me afeard.
Why are they running away? This is a trick of theirs to scare me.
O Bottom, thou art changed! What do I see on thee?
Oh, Bottom, you've changed! What's that I see on you?
What do you see? You see an ass-head of your own, do you?
What do you see? You see an ass's head of your own, do you?
Bless thee, Bottom! bless thee! Thou art translated.
God bless you, Bottom! God bless you! You've been transformed.

I see their knavery. This is to make an ass of me, to fright me, if / they could. But I will not stir from this place, do what they can. I / will walk up and down here, and I will sing, that they shall hear I am / not afraid. / [Sings] / The ousel cock, so black of hue, / With orange-tawny bill, / The throstle with his note so true, / The wren with little quill.

I see their trick. This is to make an ass of me, to frighten me if they could. But I won't move from this spot, whatever they do. I'll walk up and down here and I'll sing, so they'll hear I'm not afraid. [He sings] The blackbird, so black in colour, with its orange-brown beak, the thrush with its song so true, the wren with its little quill.
[Waking] What angel wakes me from my flowery bed?
What angel wakes me from my bed of flowers?

[Sings] / The finch, the sparrow, and the lark, / The plain-song cuckoo gray, / Whose note full many a man doth mark, / And dares not answer nay. / for, indeed, who would set his wit to so foolish a bird? Who would give / a bird the lie, though he cry 'cuckoo' never so?

The finch, the sparrow and the lark, the grey cuckoo with its simple song, whose call many a man hears and dares not deny. Because, honestly, who would waste his brains answering such a foolish bird? Who would call a bird a liar, however often it cries 'cuckoo'?

I pray thee, gentle mortal, sing again. / Mine ear is much enamour'd of thy note. / So is mine eye enthrallèd to thy shape; / And thy fair virtue's force perforce doth move me, / On the first view, to say, to swear, I love thee.

Please, gentle mortal, sing again. My ear is in love with your song. And my eye is enchanted by your shape, and the power of your fine qualities forces me, at first sight, to say, to swear, that I love you.

Methinks, mistress, you should have little reason for that. And yet, to / say the truth, reason and love keep little company together nowadays. / The more the pity that some honest neighbours will not make them / friends. Nay, I can gleek upon occasion.

I think, madam, you have very little reason for that. And yet, to tell the truth, reason and love don't spend much time together these days. It's a pity some honest neighbour doesn't make them friends. There, I can make a clever joke when I want to.
Thou art as wise as thou art beautiful.
You are as wise as you are beautiful.
Not so, neither; but if I had wit enough to get out of this wood, I / have enough to serve mine own turn.
No, I'm not. But if I had the brains to get out of this wood, I'd have enough for what I need.

Out of this wood do not desire to go. / Thou shalt remain here whether thou wilt or no. / I am a spirit of no common rate. / The summer still doth tend upon my state; / And I do love thee: therefore, go with me. / I'll give thee fairies to attend on thee; / And they shall fetch thee jewels from the deep, / And sing, while thou on pressèd flowers dost sleep. / And I will purge thy mortal grossness so / That thou shalt like an airy spirit go.— / Peaseblossom! Cobweb! Moth! and Mustardseed!

Don't wish to leave this wood. You will stay here whether you want to or not. I am no ordinary spirit. Summer itself always waits on me as its queen, and I love you. So come with me. I'll give you fairies to serve you, and they will fetch you jewels from the bottom of the sea and sing while you sleep on a bed of flowers. And I will clean away your mortal heaviness so that you can move like an airy spirit. Peaseblossom! Cobweb! Moth! And Mustardseed!

Be kind and courteous to this gentleman; / Hop in his walks and gambol in his eyes; / Feed him with apricocks and dewberries, / With purple grapes, green figs, and mulberries; / The honey-bags steal from the humble-bees, / And for night-tapers, crop their waxen thighs, / And light them at the fiery glow-worm's eyes, / To have my love to bed and to arise; / And pluck the wings from painted butterflies, / To fan the moonbeams from his sleeping eyes. / Nod to him, elves, and do him courtesies.

Be kind and polite to this gentleman. Hop where he walks and dance in front of his eyes. Feed him with apricots and blackberries, purple grapes, green figs and mulberries. Steal the honey-sacs from the bumblebees, and for candles, take the wax from their legs and light them from the fiery eyes of glow-worms, to light my love to bed and to wake him. And pull the wings off painted butterflies to fan the moonlight away from his sleeping eyes. Bow to him, elves, and pay him your respects.
I cry your worships mercy, heartily.—I beseech your worship's name.
I humbly beg your worships' pardon. Please may I ask your worship's name?
I shall desire you of more acquaintance, good Master Cobweb. If I cut / my finger, I shall make bold with you.—Your name, honest gentleman?
I hope to get to know you better, good Master Cobweb. If I cut my finger, I'll make use of you. Your name, honest gentleman?
I pray you, commend me to Mistress Squash, your mother, and to Master / Peascod, your father. Good Master Peaseblossom, I shall desire you of / more acquaintance too.—Your name, I beseech you, sir?
