Please give my regards to Mrs Squash, your mother, and Mr Peascod, your father. Good Master Peaseblossom, I hope to know you better too. Your name, please, sir?

Good Master Mustardseed, I know your patience well. That same cowardly / giant-like ox-beef hath devoured many a gentleman of your house. I / promise you, your kindred hath made my eyes water ere now. I desire you / of more acquaintance, good Master Mustardseed.

Good Master Mustardseed, I know all about your suffering. That cowardly, giant-sized roast beef has eaten many gentlemen of your family. I promise you, your relatives have made my eyes water before now. I hope to know you better, good Master Mustardseed.

Come, wait upon him; lead him to my bower. / The moon, methinks, looks with a watery eye, / And when she weeps, weeps every little flower, / Lamenting some enforced chastity. / Tie up my love's tongue, bring him silently.

Come, attend to him. Lead him to my bower. The moon looks to me as if her eyes are wet, and when she cries, every little flower cries too, mourning some girl's lost virginity. Tie up my love's tongue. Bring him quietly.
I wonder if Titania be awak'd; / Then, what it was that next came in her eye, / Which she must dote on in extremity.
I wonder if Titania has woken up, and what was the first thing she saw, which she must now love to distraction.
Here comes my messenger. How now, mad spirit? / What night-rule now about this haunted grove?
Here comes my messenger. Well, crazy spirit? What night-time mischief is going on in this haunted wood?

My mistress with a monster is in love. / Near to her close and consecrated bower, / While she was in her dull and sleeping hour, / A crew of patches, rude mechanicals, / That work for bread upon Athenian stalls, / Were met together to rehearse a play / Intended for great Theseus' nuptial day. / The shallowest thick-skin of that barren sort / Who Pyramus presented in their sport, / Forsook his scene and enter'd in a brake. / When I did him at this advantage take, / An ass's nole I fixed on his head. / Anon, his Thisbe must be answerèd, / And forth my mimic comes. When they him spy, / As wild geese that the creeping fowler eye, / Or russet-pated choughs, many in sort, / Rising and cawing at the gun's report, / Sever themselves and madly sweep the sky, / So at his sight away his fellows fly, / And at our stamp, here o'er and o'er one falls; / He murder cries, and help from Athens calls. / Their sense thus weak, lost with their fears, thus strong, / Made senseless things begin to do them wrong; / For briers and thorns at their apparel snatch; / Some sleeves, some hats, from yielders all things catch. / I led them on in this distracted fear, / And left sweet Pyramus translated there. / When in that moment, so it came to pass, / Titania wak'd, and straightway lov'd an ass.

My mistress is in love with a monster. Near her private, sacred bower, while she was sleeping, a gang of fools, rough workmen who earn their bread in the Athenian market, met to rehearse a play they are planning for great Theseus's wedding day. The stupidest blockhead of that brainless lot, who played Pyramus in their show, left his scene and went into a thicket. When I caught him there, I fixed an ass's head on him. Soon he had to answer his Thisbe, and out comes my actor. When they saw him, like wild geese that spot the hunter creeping up, or a big flock of grey-headed jackdaws rising and cawing at the sound of a gun and scattering wildly across the sky, his friends ran away at the sight of him. And when I stamped my foot, one after another fell over. One shouted 'Murder!' and called to Athens for help. Their wits were so weak, and their fears so strong, that lifeless things began to attack them: briars and thorns snatched at their clothes, a sleeve here, a hat there. Everything grabs from a man who gives in. I led them on in this crazy fear, and left sweet Pyramus, transformed, behind. At that very moment, as it happened, Titania woke and immediately fell in love with an ass.
This falls out better than I could devise. / But hast thou yet latch'd the Athenian's eyes / With the love-juice, as I did bid thee do?
This has turned out better than I could have planned. But have you put the love-juice on the Athenian's eyes, as I told you to?
I took him sleeping—that is finish'd too— / And the Athenian woman by his side, / That, when he wak'd, of force she must be ey'd.
I caught him sleeping. That's done too. And the Athenian woman was beside him, so that when he wakes, he's bound to see her.
Stand close. This is the same Athenian.
Keep out of sight. This is the same Athenian.
This is the woman, but not this the man.
This is the woman, but that's not the man.
O why rebuke you him that loves you so? / Lay breath so bitter on your bitter foe.
Oh, why do you scold a man who loves you so much? Save such bitter words for your bitter enemy.

Now I but chide, but I should use thee worse, / For thou, I fear, hast given me cause to curse. / If thou hast slain Lysander in his sleep, / Being o'er shoes in blood, plunge in the deep, / And kill me too. / The sun was not so true unto the day / As he to me. Would he have stol'n away / From sleeping Hermia? I'll believe as soon / This whole earth may be bor'd, and that the moon / May through the centre creep and so displease / Her brother's noontide with th' Antipodes. / It cannot be but thou hast murder'd him. / So should a murderer look, so dead, so grim.

For now I'm only scolding you, but I ought to treat you worse, because I'm afraid you've given me reason to curse you. If you've killed Lysander in his sleep, you're already ankle-deep in blood, so wade in deeper and kill me too. The sun was never as faithful to the day as he was to me. Would he have crept away from Hermia while she was asleep? I'd sooner believe that a hole could be drilled through the earth, and that the moon could creep through it and annoy her brother the sun at noon on the other side of the world. You must have murdered him. That's how a murderer looks, so deathly pale, so grim.
So should the murder'd look, and so should I, / Pierc'd through the heart with your stern cruelty. / Yet you, the murderer, look as bright, as clear, / As yonder Venus in her glimmering sphere.
That's how the murdered man looks, and that's how I look, stabbed through the heart by your harsh cruelty. Yet you, the murderer, look as bright and clear as Venus, shining up there in her orbit.
What's this to my Lysander? Where is he? / Ah, good Demetrius, wilt thou give him me?
What has this got to do with my Lysander? Where is he? Oh, good Demetrius, will you give him back to me?
I had rather give his carcass to my hounds.
I'd rather give his dead body to my dogs.

Out, dog! Out, cur! Thou driv'st me past the bounds / Of maiden's patience. Hast thou slain him, then? / Henceforth be never number'd among men! / O once tell true; tell true, even for my sake! / Durst thou have look'd upon him, being awake, / And hast thou kill'd him sleeping? O brave touch! / Could not a worm, an adder, do so much? / An adder did it; for with doubler tongue / Than thine, thou serpent, never adder stung.

Get out, dog! Get out, cur! You're driving me past the limits of a girl's patience. So have you killed him? From now on, don't ever count yourself a man! Oh, tell the truth for once, tell the truth, even if only for my sake! Would you have dared to look at him while he was awake, and did you kill him while he slept? Oh, how brave! Couldn't a worm or a snake do as much? A snake did do it, because no snake ever stung with a more forked tongue than yours, you serpent.
You spend your passion on a mispris'd mood: / I am not guilty of Lysander's blood; / Nor is he dead, for aught that I can tell.
You're wasting your anger on a mistake. I'm not guilty of Lysander's blood, and he isn't dead, as far as I know.
I pray thee, tell me then that he is well.
Then please tell me he's all right.
And if I could, what should I get therefore?
And if I could, what would I get for it?
A privilege never to see me more. / And from thy hated presence part I so: / See me no more, whether he be dead or no.
The privilege of never seeing me again. And so I leave your hateful company. Don't see me again, whether he's dead or not.

There is no following her in this fierce vein. / Here, therefore, for a while I will remain. / So sorrow's heaviness doth heavier grow / For debt that bankrupt sleep doth sorrow owe; / Which now in some slight measure it will pay, / If for his tender here I make some stay.

There's no point following her while she's in this furious mood. So I'll stay here for a while. Sorrow gets heavier when sleep, like a bankrupt, can't pay what it owes. Now sleep will pay back a little of its debt, if I stay here and accept its offer.
What hast thou done? Thou hast mistaken quite, / And laid the love-juice on some true-love's sight. / Of thy misprision must perforce ensue / Some true love turn'd, and not a false turn'd true.
What have you done? You've made a complete mistake and put the love-juice on the eyes of someone truly in love. Your error is bound to turn a true love false, instead of a false love true.
Then fate o'er-rules, that, one man holding troth, / A million fail, confounding oath on oath.
Then fate has taken over: for every man who keeps his promise, a million fail, breaking oath after oath.

About the wood go swifter than the wind, / And Helena of Athens look thou find. / All fancy-sick she is, and pale of cheer / With sighs of love, that costs the fresh blood dear. / By some illusion see thou bring her here; / I'll charm his eyes against she do appear.

Go round the wood faster than the wind, and make sure you find Helena of Athens. She is lovesick and pale-faced from the sighs of love, which drain away the fresh blood. Bring her here with some trick. I'll put a spell on his eyes ready for when she appears.
I go, I go; look how I go, / Swifter than arrow from the Tartar's bow.
I'm going, I'm going. Look how I go, faster than an arrow from a Tartar's bow.

Flower of this purple dye, / Hit with Cupid's archery, / Sink in apple of his eye. / When his love he doth espy, / Let her shine as gloriously / As the Venus of the sky.— / When thou wak'st, if she be by, / Beg of her for remedy.

Flower with this purple colour, struck by Cupid's arrow, sink into the pupil of his eye. When he sees his love, let her shine as brilliantly as Venus in the sky. When you wake, if she is near, beg her to cure you.
Captain of our fairy band, / Helena is here at hand, / And the youth mistook by me, / Pleading for a lover's fee. / Shall we their fond pageant see? / Lord, what fools these mortals be!
Captain of our fairy army, Helena is close by, and the young man I made the mistake with, begging her to love him. Shall we watch their silly show? Lord, what fools these mortals are!
Stand aside. The noise they make / Will cause Demetrius to awake.
Stand aside. The noise they're making will wake Demetrius.
Then will two at once woo one. / That must needs be sport alone; / And those things do best please me / That befall prepost'rously.
Then two will be courting one at the same time. That will be fun all on its own. And the things that please me best are the ones that turn out all upside down.

Why should you think that I should woo in scorn? / Scorn and derision never come in tears. / Look when I vow, I weep; and vows so born, / In their nativity all truth appears. / How can these things in me seem scorn to you, / Bearing the badge of faith, to prove them true?

Why should you think I'm courting you to mock you? Mockery and scorn never come with tears. Look, when I make a promise, I cry, and promises born like that show they are true from the moment they're made. How can these things look like mockery to you, when they carry the proof of faithfulness, my tears, to show they're real?

You do advance your cunning more and more. / When truth kills truth, O devilish-holy fray! / These vows are Hermia's: will you give her o'er? / Weigh oath with oath, and you will nothing weigh: / Your vows to her and me, put in two scales, / Will even weigh; and both as light as tales.

You're showing your cunning more and more. When one truth kills another, what a devilish holy fight! These promises belong to Hermia. Will you give her up? Weigh one promise against the other and you'll find they weigh nothing. Your promises to her and to me, put on two sides of a scale, will balance, and both are as light as fairy tales.
I had no judgment when to her I swore.
I had no judgement when I made promises to her.
Nor none, in my mind, now you give her o'er.
And you have none now, I think, when you give her up.
Demetrius loves her, and he loves not you.
Demetrius loves her, and he doesn't love you.

[Waking] O Helen, goddess, nymph, perfect, divine! / To what, my love, shall I compare thine eyne? / Crystal is muddy. O how ripe in show / Thy lips, those kissing cherries, tempting grow! / That pure congealèd white, high Taurus' snow, / Fann'd with the eastern wind, turns to a crow / When thou hold'st up thy hand. O, let me kiss / This princess of pure white, this seal of bliss!

Oh Helena, goddess, nymph, perfect, divine! What can I compare your eyes to, my love? Crystal looks muddy beside them. Oh, how ripe and tempting your lips look, those kissing cherries! That pure, frozen white snow on the high Taurus mountains, blown by the east wind, looks as black as a crow when you hold up your hand. Oh, let me kiss this princess of pure whiteness, this promise of happiness!

O spite! O hell! I see you all are bent / To set against me for your merriment. / If you were civil, and knew courtesy, / You would not do me thus much injury. / Can you not hate me, as I know you do, / But you must join in souls to mock me too? / If you were men, as men you are in show, / You would not use a gentle lady so; / To vow, and swear, and superpraise my parts, / When I am sure you hate me with your hearts. / You both are rivals, and love Hermia; / And now both rivals, to mock Helena. / A trim exploit, a manly enterprise, / To conjure tears up in a poor maid's eyes / With your derision! None of noble sort / Would so offend a virgin, and extort / A poor soul's patience, all to make you sport.

How cruel! What hell! I can see you're all determined to gang up on me for your entertainment. If you were decent and had any manners, you wouldn't hurt me like this. Isn't it enough to hate me, as I know you do, without joining forces to mock me as well? If you were real men, as you look like men, you wouldn't treat a gentle lady like this: promising, swearing and overpraising my looks, when I'm sure you hate me with all your hearts. You're both rivals in love with Hermia, and now you're rivals in mocking Helena. A fine achievement, a manly deed, to bring tears to a poor girl's eyes with your scorn! No one of noble birth would insult a girl like that and push a poor soul's patience to breaking point, just to amuse yourselves.

You are unkind, Demetrius; be not so, / For you love Hermia; this you know I know. / And here, with all good will, with all my heart, / In Hermia's love I yield you up my part; / And yours of Helena to me bequeath, / Whom I do love and will do till my death.

You're being unkind, Demetrius. Don't be like that, because you love Hermia; you know I know that. And here, with all my good will, with all my heart, I give you my share of Hermia's love. In return, give me your share of Helena, whom I love and will love until I die.
Never did mockers waste more idle breath.
Mockers never wasted so much useless breath.
Lysander, keep thy Hermia; I will none. / If e'er I lov'd her, all that love is gone. / My heart to her but as guest-wise sojourn'd; / And now to Helen is it home return'd, / There to remain.
Lysander, keep your Hermia. I don't want her. If I ever loved her, all that love has gone. My heart only stayed with her like a visitor, and now it has come home to Helena, to stay there.
Disparage not the faith thou dost not know, / Lest to thy peril thou aby it dear. / Look where thy love comes; yonder is thy dear.
Don't run down a love you know nothing about, or you'll pay dearly for it. Look, here comes your love. There's your darling.

Dark night, that from the eye his function takes, / The ear more quick of apprehension makes; / Wherein it doth impair the seeing sense, / It pays the hearing double recompense. / Thou art not by mine eye, Lysander, found; / Mine ear, I thank it, brought me to thy sound. / But why unkindly didst thou leave me so?

Dark night, which takes away the eye's power to see, makes the ear quicker to hear. While it weakens our sight, it pays the hearing back twice over. My eyes couldn't find you, Lysander. My ear, I thank it, led me to the sound of your voice. But why did you leave me so cruelly?
Why should he stay whom love doth press to go?
Why should someone stay when love urges him to go?
What love could press Lysander from my side?
What love could drive Lysander from my side?

Lysander's love, that would not let him bide, / Fair Helena, who more engilds the night / Than all yon fiery oes and eyes of light. / Why seek'st thou me? Could not this make thee know / The hate I bare thee made me leave thee so?

Lysander's love, which wouldn't let him stay: beautiful Helena, who brightens the night more than all those fiery circles and eyes of light up there. Why are you looking for me? Didn't this make you realise that it was because I hate you that I left you like that?
You speak not as you think; it cannot be.
You don't mean what you're saying. It can't be true.

Lo, she is one of this confederacy! / Now I perceive they have conjoin'd all three / To fashion this false sport in spite of me. / Injurious Hermia, most ungrateful maid! / Have you conspir'd, have you with these contriv'd, / To bait me with this foul derision? / Is all the counsel that we two have shar'd, / The sisters' vows, the hours that we have spent, / When we have chid the hasty-footed time / For parting us—O, is all forgot? / All school-days' friendship, childhood innocence? / We, Hermia, like two artificial gods, / Have with our needles created both one flower, / Both on one sampler, sitting on one cushion, / Both warbling of one song, both in one key, / As if our hands, our sides, voices, and minds, / Had been incorporate. So we grew together, / Like to a double cherry, seeming parted, / But yet a union in partition, / Two lovely berries moulded on one stem; / So, with two seeming bodies, but one heart; / Two of the first, like coats in heraldry, / Due but to one, and crownèd with one crest. / And will you rent our ancient love asunder, / To join with men in scorning your poor friend? / It is not friendly, 'tis not maidenly. / Our sex, as well as I, may chide you for it, / Though I alone do feel the injury.

Look, she's part of this plot too! Now I see they've all three joined together to set up this cruel game to spite me. Hurtful Hermia, most ungrateful girl! Have you plotted, have you schemed with these men, to torment me with this foul mockery? Have all the secrets we two shared, the vows we made as sisters, the hours we spent together, when we scolded time for hurrying to part us, oh, have they all been forgotten? All our schooldays' friendship, our childhood innocence? Hermia, we were like two creative gods. With our needles we both made one flower, both sewing on one sampler, sitting on one cushion, both singing one song, both in the same key, as if our hands, our bodies, voices and minds were all one. So we grew up together like a double cherry, which looks like two but is joined though divided, two lovely berries growing on one stem. So we were two bodies with one heart, like the two halves of a coat of arms that belong to one family and are topped by one crest. And will you tear our old love apart, to join with men in mocking your poor friend? It isn't friendly. It isn't the way a girl should behave. All women, as well as me, could blame you for it, though I am the only one who feels the hurt.
I am amazèd at your passionate words: / I scorn you not; it seems that you scorn me.
Your passionate words amaze me. I'm not mocking you. It seems that you are mocking me.

Have you not set Lysander, as in scorn, / To follow me, and praise my eyes and face? / And made your other love, Demetrius, / Who even but now did spurn me with his foot, / To call me goddess, nymph, divine and rare, / Precious, celestial? Wherefore speaks he this / To her he hates? And wherefore doth Lysander / Deny your love, so rich within his soul, / And tender me, forsooth, affection, / But by your setting on, by your consent? / What though I be not so in grace as you, / So hung upon with love, so fortunate, / But miserable most, to love unlov'd? / This you should pity rather than despise.

Haven't you sent Lysander to follow me, to mock me, and praise my eyes and face? And made your other lover, Demetrius, who only just now kicked me away with his foot, call me goddess, nymph, divine, wonderful, precious, heavenly? Why does he say this to a woman he hates? And why does Lysander deny his love for you, which is so rich in his soul, and offer me, of all things, his affection, unless you put him up to it and agreed to it? So what if I'm not as popular as you, not as surrounded by love, not as lucky, but most miserable, loving and not being loved? You should pity this, not despise it.
I understand not what you mean by this.
I don't understand what you mean by this.

Ay, do. Persever, counterfeit sad looks, / Make mouths upon me when I turn my back, / Wink each at other; hold the sweet jest up. / This sport, well carried, shall be chronicled. / If you have any pity, grace, or manners, / You would not make me such an argument. / But fare ye well. 'Tis partly my own fault, / Which death, or absence, soon shall remedy.

Oh yes, carry on. Keep pretending to look serious, pull faces at me when I turn my back, wink at each other, keep up your sweet joke. This game, if you play it well, will go down in history. If you had any pity, kindness or manners, you wouldn't make me the butt of your joke like this. But goodbye. It's partly my own fault, and death or going away will soon fix that.
Stay, gentle Helena; hear my excuse; / My love, my life, my soul, fair Helena!
Stay, gentle Helena, and hear me explain. My love, my life, my soul, beautiful Helena!
Sweet, do not scorn her so.
Sweetheart, don't mock her like that.
If she cannot entreat, I can compel.
If she can't persuade you to stop, I can force you.

Thou canst compel no more than she entreat; / Thy threats have no more strength than her weak prayers. / Helen, I love thee, by my life I do; / I swear by that which I will lose for thee / To prove him false that says I love thee not.

You can no more force me than she can persuade me. Your threats have no more strength than her weak pleas. Helena, I love you. By my life, I do. I swear by my life, which I'm ready to lose for you, to prove wrong any man who says I don't love you.
I say I love thee more than he can do.
I say I love you more than he can.
If thou say so, withdraw, and prove it too.
If you say so, come away and prove it.
Lysander, where is all this leading?
No, no. He will / Seem to break loose. Take on as you would follow, / But yet come not. You are a tame man, go!
No, no. He'll pretend to break free. Make a show as if you're going to follow me, but then don't come. You're a coward. Go on!
Hang off, thou cat, thou burr! Vile thing, let loose, / Or I will shake thee from me like a serpent.
Let go, you cat, you burr! Vile thing, let go, or I'll shake you off me like a snake.
Why are you grown so rude? What change is this, / Sweet love?
Why have you become so rough? What's changed, sweet love?
Thy love? Out, tawny Tartar, out! / Out, loathèd medicine! O hated potion, hence!
Your love? Get away, you dark-skinned Tartar, get away! Get away, disgusting medicine! Hateful poison, get away!
Yes, sooth, and so do you.
Yes, he is, and so are you.
Demetrius, I will keep my word with thee.
Demetrius, I'll keep my promise to you.
I would I had your bond; for I perceive / A weak bond holds you; I'll not trust your word.
I wish I had your promise in writing, because I can see a weak bond is holding you. I won't trust your word.
What, should I hurt her, strike her, kill her dead? / Although I hate her, I'll not harm her so.
What, should I hurt her, hit her, kill her? Although I hate her, I won't harm her like that.

What, can you do me greater harm than hate? / Hate me? Wherefore? O me! what news, my love? / Am not I Hermia? Are not you Lysander? / I am as fair now as I was erewhile. / Since night you lov'd me; yet since night you left me. / Why then, you left me—O, the gods forbid!— / In earnest, shall I say?

What, can you do me any greater harm than hating me? Hate me? Why? Oh no! What's happened, my love? Aren't I Hermia? Aren't you Lysander? I'm as beautiful now as I was a while ago. You loved me at nightfall, and yet during the night you left me. So did you leave me (oh, the gods forbid!) in earnest, shall I say?
Ay, by my life; / And never did desire to see thee more. / Therefore be out of hope, of question, of doubt; / Be certain, nothing truer; 'tis no jest / That I do hate thee and love Helena.
Yes, I swear on my life, and I never wanted to see you again. So give up hope, give up questions, give up doubt. Be certain, nothing is truer: it's no joke that I hate you and love Helena.
O me! You juggler! You cankerblossom! / You thief of love! What! have you come by night / And stol'n my love's heart from him?
Oh no! You trickster! You grub that eats flowers! You thief of love! What, have you come in the night and stolen my love's heart from him?
Fine, i' faith! / Have you no modesty, no maiden shame, / No touch of bashfulness? What, will you tear / Impatient answers from my gentle tongue? / Fie, fie, you counterfeit, you puppet, you!
That's rich, really! Have you no modesty, no shame, not a trace of shyness? What, are you going to force angry answers out of my gentle mouth? Shame on you, you fake, you puppet, you!

Puppet! Why so? Ay, that way goes the game. / Now I perceive that she hath made compare / Between our statures; she hath urg'd her height; / And with her personage, her tall personage, / Her height, forsooth, she hath prevail'd with him. / And are you grown so high in his esteem / Because I am so dwarfish and so low? / How low am I, thou painted maypole? Speak, / How low am I? I am not yet so low / But that my nails can reach unto thine eyes.

Puppet? Why puppet? Oh, so that's the game. Now I see she's been comparing our heights. She's made a point of how tall she is, and with her figure, her tall figure, her height, if you please, she has won him over. And have you grown so high in his opinion because I'm so short and dwarfish? How short am I, you painted maypole? Tell me, how short am I? I'm not so short that my nails can't reach your eyes.

I pray you, though you mock me, gentlemen, / Let her not hurt me. I was never curst; / I have no gift at all in shrewishness; / I am a right maid for my cowardice; / Let her not strike me. You perhaps may think, / Because she is something lower than myself, / That I can match her.

Please, gentlemen, even if you are mocking me, don't let her hurt me. I was never bad-tempered. I have no talent at all for being a shrew. I'm a real girl when it comes to being a coward. Don't let her hit me. You might think, because she's a bit shorter than me, that I can fight her.
Shorter! Listen, she's said it again!

Good Hermia, do not be so bitter with me. / I evermore did love you, Hermia, / Did ever keep your counsels, never wrong'd you, / Save that, in love unto Demetrius, / I told him of your stealth unto this wood. / He follow'd you; for love I follow'd him; / But he hath chid me hence, and threaten'd me / To strike me, spurn me, nay, to kill me too: / And now, so you will let me quiet go, / To Athens will I bear my folly back, / And follow you no further. Let me go: / You see how simple and how fond I am.

Good Hermia, don't be so bitter with me. I always loved you, Hermia, always kept your secrets, never wronged you, except that, out of love for Demetrius, I told him you were slipping away to this wood. He followed you, and out of love I followed him. But he has scolded me and sent me away, and threatened to hit me, kick me, even to kill me. So now, if you'll let me go quietly, I'll take my foolishness back to Athens and follow you no further. Let me go. You can see how simple and foolish I am.
Why, get you gone. Who is't that hinders you?
Well, go then. Who's stopping you?
A foolish heart that I leave here behind.
A foolish heart that I'm leaving behind here.
Be not afraid; she shall not harm thee, Helena.
Don't be afraid. She won't hurt you, Helena.
No, sir, she shall not, though you take her part.
No, sir, she won't, even if you take her side.
O, when she's angry, she is keen and shrewd. / She was a vixen when she went to school, / And though she be but little, she is fierce.
Oh, when she's angry, she's sharp and vicious. She was a little vixen at school, and though she's only small, she's fierce.
Little again! Nothing but low and little? / Why will you suffer her to flout me thus? / Let me come to her.
Small again! Nothing but short and small? Why do you let her insult me like this? Let me get at her.
Get you gone, you dwarf; / You minimus, of hind'ring knot-grass made; / You bead, you acorn.
Get away, you dwarf, you tiny thing, made of knot-grass that stunts growth. You bead, you acorn!

You are too officious / In her behalf that scorns your services. / Let her alone. Speak not of Helena; / Take not her part; for if thou dost intend / Never so little show of love to her, / Thou shalt aby it.
You're too eager to help a woman who scorns your services. Leave her alone. Don't talk about Helena. Don't take her side. Because if you try to show her even the slightest love, you'll pay for it.
Now she holds me not. / Now follow, if thou dar'st, to try whose right, / Of thine or mine, is most in Helena.
Now she's not holding me. Now follow me, if you dare, to find out whose claim to Helena is stronger, yours or mine.
Follow! Nay, I'll go with thee, cheek by jole.
Follow you? No, I'll go right beside you, cheek by jowl.
You, mistress, all this coil is long of you. / Nay, go not back.
You, madam, all this trouble is because of you. No, don't back away.
I will not trust you, I, / Nor longer stay in your curst company. / Your hands than mine are quicker for a fray. / My legs are longer though, to run away.
I won't trust you, not me, and I won't stay any longer in your bad-tempered company. Your hands are quicker than mine in a fight, but my legs are longer for running away.
I am amaz'd, and know not what to say.
I'm stunned, and I don't know what to say.
This is thy negligence: still thou mistak'st, / Or else commit'st thy knaveries willfully.
This is your carelessness. You're always making mistakes, or else you play your tricks on purpose.

Believe me, king of shadows, I mistook. / Did not you tell me I should know the man / By the Athenian garments he had on? / And so far blameless proves my enterprise / That I have 'nointed an Athenian's eyes: / And so far am I glad it so did sort, / As this their jangling I esteem a sport.

Believe me, king of shadows, I made a mistake. Didn't you tell me I would recognise the man by the Athenian clothes he was wearing? So far my work has been blameless, because I did put the juice on an Athenian's eyes. And so far I'm glad it turned out this way, because I think their squabbling is great fun.

Thou seest these lovers seek a place to fight. / Hie therefore, Robin, overcast the night; / The starry welkin cover thou anon / With drooping fog, as black as Acheron, / And lead these testy rivals so astray / As one come not within another's way. / Like to Lysander sometime frame thy tongue, / Then stir Demetrius up with bitter wrong; / And sometime rail thou like Demetrius. / And from each other look thou lead them thus, / Till o'er their brows death-counterfeiting sleep / With leaden legs and batty wings doth creep. / Then crush this herb into Lysander's eye, / Whose liquor hath this virtuous property, / To take from thence all error with his might / And make his eyeballs roll with wonted sight. / When they next wake, all this derision / Shall seem a dream and fruitless vision; / And back to Athens shall the lovers wend, / With league whose date till death shall never end. / Whiles I in this affair do thee employ, / I'll to my queen, and beg her Indian boy; / And then I will her charmèd eye release / From monster's view, and all things shall be peace.

You can see these lovers are looking for a place to fight. So hurry, Robin, and cloud over the night. Cover the starry sky straight away with a low fog as black as hell's river, and lead these angry rivals so far astray that neither can find the other. Sometimes imitate Lysander's voice and stir Demetrius up with cruel insults, and sometimes rant like Demetrius. Lead them away from each other like this until sleep, which looks like death, creeps over their foreheads with legs as heavy as lead and wings like a bat's. Then squeeze this herb into Lysander's eye. Its juice has the power to take away all his error and make his eyes see as they used to. When they next wake, all this foolishness will seem like a dream, an empty vision, and the lovers will go back to Athens, joined in a bond that will last until death. While I give you this job, I'll go to my queen and ask her for her Indian boy. And then I'll free her bewitched eyes from the sight of that monster, and everything will be peaceful.

My fairy lord, this must be done with haste, / For night's swift dragons cut the clouds full fast; / And yonder shines Aurora's harbinger, / At whose approach, ghosts wandering here and there / Troop home to churchyards. Damnèd spirits all, / That in cross-ways and floods have burial, / Already to their wormy beds are gone; / For fear lest day should look their shames upon, / They wilfully themselves exile from light, / And must for aye consort with black-brow'd night.

My fairy lord, this has to be done quickly, because night's swift dragons are cutting through the clouds at full speed, and over there shines the morning star that announces the dawn. When it comes, ghosts wandering here and there flock home to the churchyards. All the damned spirits buried at crossroads or drowned in rivers have already gone to their beds of worms. Afraid that daylight might see their shame, they shut themselves away from the light on purpose, and must keep company for ever with dark-browed night.

But we are spirits of another sort: / I with the morning's love have oft made sport; / And, like a forester, the groves may tread / Even till the eastern gate, all fiery-red, / Opening on Neptune with fair blessèd beams, / Turns into yellow gold his salt-green streams. / But, notwithstanding, haste, make no delay. / We may effect this business yet ere day.

But we are a different kind of spirit. I have often played with the lover of the morning, and like a forester I can walk the woods right up until the gates of the east, fiery red, open onto the sea with lovely blessed rays and turn its salty green waves to yellow gold. But all the same, hurry. Don't delay. We can still get this done before daybreak.
Up and down, up and down, / I will lead them up and down. / I am fear'd in field and town. / Goblin, lead them up and down. / Here comes one.
Up and down, up and down, I will lead them up and down. I am feared in country and town. Goblin, lead them up and down. Here comes one.
Where art thou, proud Demetrius? Speak thou now.
Where are you, proud Demetrius? Speak now.
Here, villain, drawn and ready. Where art thou?
Here, villain, with my sword drawn and ready. Where are you?
I will be with thee straight.
I'll be with you in a moment.
Follow me then to plainer ground.
Follow me, then, to more level ground.
Lysander, speak again. / Thou runaway, thou coward, art thou fled? / Speak. In some bush? Where dost thou hide thy head?
Lysander, speak again! You runaway, you coward, have you run off? Speak! In some bush? Where are you hiding your head?

Thou coward, art thou bragging to the stars, / Telling the bushes that thou look'st for wars, / And wilt not come? Come, recreant, come, thou child! / I'll whip thee with a rod. He is defil'd / That draws a sword on thee.

You coward, are you boasting to the stars, telling the bushes that you're looking for a fight, and won't come? Come on, you traitor, come on, you child! I'll beat you with a stick. It's a disgrace to draw a sword on you.
Follow my voice; we'll try no manhood here.
Follow my voice. This is no place to test our courage.

He goes before me, and still dares me on; / When I come where he calls, then he is gone. / The villain is much lighter-heel'd than I: / I follow'd fast, but faster he did fly, / That fallen am I in dark uneven way, / And here will rest me. Come, thou gentle day! / [Lies down] For if but once thou show me thy grey light, / I'll find Demetrius, and revenge this spite.

He goes ahead of me and keeps daring me to follow. When I get to where he calls from, he's gone. The villain is much quicker on his feet than I am. I followed fast, but he ran faster, so now I've ended up on dark, rough ground, and I'll rest here. Come, gentle day! [He lies down] As soon as you show me your grey light, I'll find Demetrius and get revenge for this insult.
Ho, ho, ho! Coward, why com'st thou not?
Ho, ho, ho! Coward, why don't you come?
Abide me, if thou dar'st; for well I wot / Thou runn'st before me, shifting every place, / And dar'st not stand, nor look me in the face. / Where art thou?
Wait for me, if you dare, because I know very well you're running ahead of me, changing places all the time, and you don't dare to stand still or look me in the face. Where are you?

Nay, then, thou mock'st me. Thou shalt buy this dear / If ever I thy face by daylight see: / Now go thy way. Faintness constraineth me / To measure out my length on this cold bed. / By day's approach look to be visited.

No, you're mocking me. You'll pay dearly for this if I ever see your face by daylight. Go your way for now. I'm so tired I have to lie down full length on this cold bed. When day comes, expect a visit from me.

O weary night, O long and tedious night, / Abate thy hours! Shine, comforts, from the east, / That I may back to Athens by daylight, / From these that my poor company detest. / And sleep, that sometimes shuts up sorrow's eye, / Steal me awhile from mine own company.

Oh weary night, oh long and boring night, make your hours shorter! Shine, comforting light, from the east, so that I can go back to Athens by daylight, away from these people who hate my poor company. And sleep, which sometimes closes the eyes of sorrow, take me away from myself for a while.
Yet but three? Come one more. / Two of both kinds makes up four. / Here she comes, curst and sad. / Cupid is a knavish lad / Thus to make poor females mad.
Only three so far? One more to come. Two of each kind make four. Here she comes, angry and sad. Cupid is a naughty boy to drive poor women mad like this.

Never so weary, never so in woe, / Bedabbled with the dew, and torn with briers, / I can no further crawl, no further go; / My legs can keep no pace with my desires. / Here will I rest me till the break of day. / Heavens shield Lysander, if they mean a fray!

I've never been so tired, never so unhappy. I'm soaked with dew and torn by briars. I can't crawl any further, can't walk any further. My legs can't keep up with what I want. I'll rest here till daybreak. Heaven protect Lysander, if they mean to fight!
On the ground / Sleep sound. / I'll apply / To your eye, / Gentle lover, remedy.
On the ground, sleep soundly. I'll put a cure on your eye, gentle lover.

When thou wak'st, / Thou tak'st / True delight / In the sight / Of thy former lady's eye. / And the country proverb known, / That every man should take his own, / In your waking shall be shown: / Jack shall have Jill; / Nought shall go ill; / The man shall have his mare again, and all shall be well.

When you wake, you'll take true delight in the sight of your old lady's eyes. And the well-known country saying, that every man should have his own, will be shown when you wake: Jack shall have Jill, nothing will go wrong, the man will get his mare back, and all will be well.
Come, sit thee down upon this flowery bed, / While I thy amiable cheeks do coy, / And stick musk-roses in thy sleek smooth head, / And kiss thy fair large ears, my gentle joy.
Come, sit down on this bed of flowers, while I stroke your lovely cheeks, and stick musk roses in your sleek, smooth head, and kiss your beautiful big ears, my gentle joy.
Scratch my head, Peaseblossom. Where's Monsieur Cobweb?
Scratch my head, Peaseblossom. Where's Monsieur Cobweb?

Monsieur Cobweb; good monsieur, get you your weapons in your hand and / kill me a red-hipped humble-bee on the top of a thistle; and, good / monsieur, bring me the honey-bag. Do not fret yourself too much in the / action, monsieur; and, good monsieur, have a care the honey-bag break / not; I would be loath to have you overflown with a honey-bag, signior. / Where's Monsieur Mustardseed?

Monsieur Cobweb, good monsieur, take your weapons in your hand and kill me a red-bottomed bumblebee on top of a thistle. And, good monsieur, bring me the honey-sac. Don't wear yourself out doing it, monsieur, and, good monsieur, take care the honey-sac doesn't burst. I'd hate to see you drowned in honey, signor. Where's Monsieur Mustardseed?
Give me your neaf, Monsieur Mustardseed. Pray you, leave your courtesy, / good monsieur.
Give me your fist, Monsieur Mustardseed. Please, stop bowing, good monsieur.

Nothing, good monsieur, but to help Cavalery Cobweb to scratch. I must / to the barber's, monsieur, for methinks I am marvellous hairy about the / face; and I am such a tender ass, if my hair do but tickle me, I must / scratch.

Nothing, good monsieur, except to help Cavalier Cobweb with the scratching. I must go to the barber's, monsieur, because I think I'm amazingly hairy about the face. And I'm such a sensitive ass that if my hair tickles me even a little, I have to scratch.
What, wilt thou hear some music, my sweet love?
Would you like to hear some music, my sweet love?
I have a reasonable good ear in music. Let us have the tongs and the / bones.
I've got a pretty good ear for music. Let's have the tongs and the bones.
Or say, sweet love, what thou desirest to eat.
Or tell me, sweet love, what you would like to eat.
Truly, a peck of provender; I could munch your good dry oats. Methinks / I have a great desire to a bottle of hay: good hay, sweet hay, hath no / fellow.
Honestly, a bucket of fodder. I could munch some of your good dry oats. I think I'd really love a bundle of hay. Good hay, sweet hay, there's nothing like it.
I have a venturous fairy that shall seek / The squirrel's hoard, and fetch thee new nuts.
I have an adventurous fairy who will find the squirrel's store and bring you fresh nuts.
I had rather have a handful or two of dried peas. But, I pray you, let / none of your people stir me; I have an exposition of sleep come upon / me.
I'd rather have a handful or two of dried peas. But please don't let any of your people disturb me. I feel an 'exposition' of sleep coming over me.

Sleep thou, and I will wind thee in my arms. / Fairies, be gone, and be all ways away. / So doth the woodbine the sweet honeysuckle / Gently entwist, the female ivy so / Enrings the barky fingers of the elm. / O, how I love thee! How I dote on thee!

Sleep, and I'll wrap you in my arms. Fairies, go away, go in every direction. This is how the bindweed gently twines round the sweet honeysuckle, and how the clinging ivy wraps round the bark-covered fingers of the elm. Oh, how I love you! How I adore you!

Welcome, good Robin. Seest thou this sweet sight? / Her dotage now I do begin to pity. / For, meeting her of late behind the wood, / Seeking sweet favours for this hateful fool, / I did upbraid her and fall out with her: / For she his hairy temples then had rounded / With coronet of fresh and fragrant flowers; / And that same dew, which sometime on the buds / Was wont to swell like round and orient pearls, / Stood now within the pretty flouriets' eyes, / Like tears that did their own disgrace bewail. / When I had at my pleasure taunted her, / And she in mild terms begg'd my patience, / I then did ask of her her changeling child; / Which straight she gave me, and her fairy sent / To bear him to my bower in fairyland. / And now I have the boy, I will undo / This hateful imperfection of her eyes. / And, gentle Puck, take this transformèd scalp / From off the head of this Athenian swain, / That he awaking when the other do, / May all to Athens back again repair, / And think no more of this night's accidents / But as the fierce vexation of a dream. / But first I will release the Fairy Queen.

Welcome, good Robin. Can you see this sweet sight? I'm beginning to pity her foolish love now. Because when I met her just now behind the wood, looking for sweet presents for this hateful fool, I told her off and quarrelled with her. She had put a crown of fresh, sweet-smelling flowers round his hairy head, and the dew that used to swell on the buds like round, shining pearls was sitting in the eyes of the pretty little flowers like tears crying over their own disgrace. When I had teased her as much as I liked, and she had gently begged me to be patient, I asked her for the stolen child. She gave him to me straight away, and sent her fairy to carry him to my bower in fairyland. And now that I have the boy, I'll undo this hateful fault in her eyes. And, gentle Puck, take this transformed head off this Athenian peasant, so that when he wakes up with the others, they can all go back to Athens and think of this night's events as nothing more than the wild torment of a dream. But first I'll free the Fairy Queen.
Be as thou wast wont to be; / See as thou was wont to see. / Dian's bud o'er Cupid's flower / Hath such force and blessed power. / Now, my Titania, wake you, my sweet queen.
Be as you used to be. See as you used to see. Diana's flower has such strength and blessed power over Cupid's flower. Now, my Titania, wake up, my sweet queen.
My Oberon, what visions have I seen! / Methought I was enamour'd of an ass.
My Oberon, what visions I've seen! I dreamed I was in love with an ass.
How came these things to pass? / O, how mine eyes do loathe his visage now!
How did this happen? Oh, how my eyes hate the sight of his face now!
Silence awhile.—Robin, take off this head. / Titania, music call; and strike more dead / Than common sleep, of all these five the sense.
Be quiet for a while. Robin, take off this head. Titania, call for music, and make these five sleep more deeply than ordinary sleep.
Music, ho, music, such as charmeth sleep.
Music, come, music, the kind that brings sleep!
Now when thou wak'st, with thine own fool's eyes peep.
Now, when you wake, see with your own fool's eyes.

Come, my queen, take hands with me, / And rock the ground whereon these sleepers be. / Now thou and I are new in amity, / And will tomorrow midnight solemnly / Dance in Duke Theseus' house triumphantly, / And bless it to all fair prosperity: / There shall the pairs of faithful lovers be / Wedded, with Theseus, all in jollity.

Come, my queen, take my hand, and let's dance and rock the ground where these sleepers lie. Now you and I are friends again, and tomorrow at midnight we will dance in Duke Theseus's house in celebration, and bless it with good fortune. There the two pairs of faithful lovers will be married, at the same time as Theseus, all in happiness.
Fairy king, attend and mark. / I do hear the morning lark.
Fairy king, listen and pay attention. I can hear the morning lark.
Then, my queen, in silence sad, / Trip we after night's shade. / We the globe can compass soon, / Swifter than the wand'ring moon.
Then, my queen, quietly and seriously, let's follow the night's shadow. We can go round the world quickly, faster than the wandering moon.
Come, my lord, and in our flight, / Tell me how it came this night / That I sleeping here was found / With these mortals on the ground.
Come, my lord, and as we fly, tell me how it happened that tonight I was found sleeping here on the ground with these mortals.

Go, one of you, find out the forester; / For now our observation is perform'd; / And since we have the vaward of the day, / My love shall hear the music of my hounds. / Uncouple in the western valley; let them go. / Dispatch I say, and find the forester.

One of you, go and find the forester. Now we have finished our May Day ceremonies, and since it is still early in the day, my love will hear the music of my hounds. Let them loose in the western valley. Let them go. Hurry, I say, and find the forester.
We will, fair queen, up to the mountain's top, / And mark the musical confusion / Of hounds and echo in conjunction.
Fair queen, we'll go up to the top of the mountain and listen to the musical confusion of the hounds and their echoes together.

I was with Hercules and Cadmus once, / When in a wood of Crete they bay'd the bear / With hounds of Sparta. Never did I hear / Such gallant chiding; for, besides the groves, / The skies, the fountains, every region near / Seem'd all one mutual cry. I never heard / So musical a discord, such sweet thunder.

I was with Hercules and Cadmus once, when they hunted a bear in a wood in Crete with Spartan hounds. I never heard such splendid barking, because the woods, the skies, the springs, the whole area round about seemed to join in one cry. I never heard such musical discord, such sweet thunder.

My hounds are bred out of the Spartan kind, / So flew'd, so sanded; and their heads are hung / With ears that sweep away the morning dew; / Crook-knee'd and dewlap'd like Thessalian bulls; / Slow in pursuit, but match'd in mouth like bells, / Each under each. A cry more tuneable / Was never holla'd to, nor cheer'd with horn, / In Crete, in Sparta, nor in Thessaly. / Judge when you hear.—But, soft, what nymphs are these?

My hounds are bred from the Spartan kind: they have the same hanging jowls and sandy colour, and their heads are hung with ears that sweep the morning dew. They are bow-legged and have folds of skin at the throat like the bulls of Thessaly. They are slow in the chase, but their voices are matched like bells, each one a note lower than the next. A more tuneful pack was never called to or cheered on with a horn in Crete, in Sparta or in Thessaly. Judge for yourself when you hear them. But wait, who are these nymphs?
My lord, this is my daughter here asleep, / And this Lysander; this Demetrius is; / This Helena, old Nedar's Helena: / I wonder of their being here together.
My lord, this is my daughter here, asleep, and this is Lysander. This is Demetrius, and this is Helena, old Nedar's Helena. I'm amazed to find them here together.

No doubt they rose up early to observe / The rite of May; and, hearing our intent, / Came here in grace of our solemnity. / But speak, Egeus; is not this the day / That Hermia should give answer of her choice?

No doubt they got up early to celebrate May Day and, hearing what we planned, came here to honour our celebrations. But tell me, Egeus, isn't this the day when Hermia has to give her answer about her choice?
Go, bid the huntsmen wake them with their horns.
Go and tell the huntsmen to wake them with their horns.
Good morrow, friends. Saint Valentine is past. / Begin these wood-birds but to couple now?
Good morning, friends. Saint Valentine's Day is long gone. Are these woodland birds only now beginning to pair up?
I pray you all, stand up. / I know you two are rival enemies. / How comes this gentle concord in the world, / That hatred is so far from jealousy / To sleep by hate, and fear no enmity?

Please, all of you, stand up. I know you two are rivals and enemies. How has such gentle harmony come into the world that hatred is so far from suspicion that it sleeps next to its enemy without fear?

My lord, I shall reply amazedly, / Half sleep, half waking; but as yet, I swear, / I cannot truly say how I came here. / But, as I think (for truly would I speak) / And now I do bethink me, so it is: / I came with Hermia hither. Our intent / Was to be gone from Athens, where we might be / Without the peril of the Athenian law.

My lord, I'll answer you in confusion, half asleep, half awake. But I swear I can't really say how I got here. But I think (because I want to tell the truth), and now that I think about it, this is how it was: I came here with Hermia. We planned to leave Athens and go where we would be safe from the Athenian law.

Enough, enough, my lord; you have enough. / I beg the law, the law upon his head. / They would have stol'n away, they would, Demetrius, / Thereby to have defeated you and me: / You of your wife, and me of my consent, / Of my consent that she should be your wife.

Enough, enough, my lord, you've heard enough. I ask for the law, the law on his head! They meant to run away, they did, Demetrius, and so cheat both you and me: cheat you of your wife, and me of my consent, my consent that she should be your wife.

My lord, fair Helen told me of their stealth, / Of this their purpose hither to this wood; / And I in fury hither follow'd them, / Fair Helena in fancy following me. / But, my good lord, I wot not by what power, / (But by some power it is) my love to Hermia, / Melted as the snow, seems to me now / As the remembrance of an idle gaud / Which in my childhood I did dote upon; / And all the faith, the virtue of my heart, / The object and the pleasure of mine eye, / Is only Helena. To her, my lord, / Was I betroth'd ere I saw Hermia. / But like a sickness did I loathe this food. / But, as in health, come to my natural taste, / Now I do wish it, love it, long for it, / And will for evermore be true to it.

My lord, beautiful Helena told me about their escape, about their plan to come here to this wood, and I followed them here in a rage, with beautiful Helena following me out of love. But, my good lord, I don't know by what power (though it must be some power) my love for Hermia has melted like snow, and now seems like the memory of some worthless toy I was obsessed with when I was a child. All the faithfulness and strength of my heart, the object and the delight of my eyes, is Helena alone. I was engaged to her, my lord, before I saw Hermia. But, like someone who is ill, I hated this food. Now, as if I were well again, my natural taste has come back. Now I want it, love it, long for it, and I will be true to it for ever.

Fair lovers, you are fortunately met. / Of this discourse we more will hear anon. / Egeus, I will overbear your will; / For in the temple, by and by with us, / These couples shall eternally be knit. / And, for the morning now is something worn, / Our purpos'd hunting shall be set aside. / Away with us to Athens. Three and three, / We'll hold a feast in great solemnity. / Come, Hippolyta.

Beautiful lovers, this is a lucky meeting. We'll hear more of this story later. Egeus, I will overrule you, because in the temple, very soon, these couples will be joined for ever together with us. And since the morning is now half gone, we'll put off our planned hunt. Come with us to Athens. Three couples together, we'll hold a grand feast. Come, Hippolyta.
These things seem small and undistinguishable, / Like far-off mountains turnèd into clouds.
These things seem small and hard to make out, like distant mountains that have turned into clouds.
Methinks I see these things with parted eye, / When everything seems double.
I feel as if I'm seeing these things with my eyes out of focus, when everything looks double.
So methinks. / And I have found Demetrius like a jewel, / Mine own, and not mine own.
So do I. And I have found Demetrius like a jewel someone has found: mine, and yet not really mine.
Are you sure / That we are awake? It seems to me / That yet we sleep, we dream. Do not you think / The Duke was here, and bid us follow him?
Are you sure we're awake? It seems to me we're still asleep and dreaming. Do you think the Duke was here and told us to follow him?
And he did bid us follow to the temple.
And he told us to follow him to the temple.
Why, then, we are awake: let's follow him, / And by the way let us recount our dreams.
Well then, we're awake. Let's follow him, and on the way let's tell each other our dreams.

[Waking] When my cue comes, call me, and I will answer. My next is / 'Most fair Pyramus.' Heigh-ho! Peter Quince! Flute, the bellows-mender! / Snout, the tinker! Starveling! God's my life! Stol'n hence, and left me / asleep! I have had a most rare vision. I have had a dream, past the wit / of man to say what dream it was. Man is but an ass if he go about to / expound this dream. Methought I was—there is no man can tell what. / Methought I was, and methought I had—but man is but a patched fool if / he will offer to say what methought I had. The eye of man hath not / heard, the ear of man hath not seen, man's hand is not able to taste, / his tongue to conceive, nor his heart to report, what my dream was. I / will get Peter Quince to write a ballad of this dream: it shall be / called 'Bottom's Dream', because it hath no bottom; and I will sing it / in the latter end of a play, before the Duke. Peradventure, to make it / the more gracious, I shall sing it at her death.

When my cue comes, call me and I'll answer. My next line is 'Most fair Pyramus.' Hey there! Peter Quince! Flute, the bellows-mender! Snout, the tinker! Starveling! God help me! They've sneaked off and left me asleep! I've had a most amazing vision. I've had a dream that no man has the brains to explain. A man would be an ass if he tried to explain this dream. I thought I was... no one can say what. I thought I was, and I thought I had... but a man would be a patched-up fool if he tried to say what I thought I had. The eye of man has never heard, the ear of man has never seen, man's hand can't taste, his tongue can't imagine, and his heart can't tell what my dream was. I'll get Peter Quince to write a ballad about this dream. It will be called 'Bottom's Dream', because it has no bottom. And I'll sing it at the end of a play, in front of the Duke. Perhaps, to make it even better, I'll sing it when Thisbe dies.
Have you sent to Bottom's house? Is he come home yet?
Have you sent someone to Bottom's house? Has he come home yet?
He cannot be heard of. Out of doubt he is transported.
No one's heard anything of him. No doubt he's been carried off.
If he come not, then the play is marred. It goes not forward, doth it?
If he doesn't come, the play's ruined. It can't go on, can it?
It is not possible. You have not a man in all Athens able to discharge / Pyramus but he.
Impossible. There's no man in all Athens who could play Pyramus except him.
No, he hath simply the best wit of any handicraft man in Athens.
No, he's simply got the best brains of any working man in Athens.
Yea, and the best person too, and he is a very paramour for a sweet / voice.
Yes, and he's the best-looking too, and he's a real lover-boy when it comes to a sweet voice.
You must say paragon. A paramour is, God bless us, a thing of naught.
You mean a 'paragon'. A 'paramour' is, God help us, a wicked thing.
Masters, the Duke is coming from the temple, and there is two or three / lords and ladies more married. If our sport had gone forward, we had / all been made men.
Gentlemen, the Duke is coming from the temple, and two or three more lords and ladies have been married too. If our play had gone ahead, our fortunes would all have been made.

O sweet bully Bottom! Thus hath he lost sixpence a day during his life; / he could not have 'scaped sixpence a day. An the Duke had not given him / sixpence a day for playing Pyramus, I'll be hanged. He would have / deserved it: sixpence a day in Pyramus, or nothing.

Oh, sweet, dear Bottom! That way he's lost a pension of sixpence a day for life. He couldn't have missed getting sixpence a day. If the Duke hadn't given him sixpence a day for playing Pyramus, I'll be hanged. He'd have deserved it: sixpence a day for Pyramus, or nothing.
Where are these lads? Where are these hearts?
Where are the lads? Where are my hearties?
Bottom! O most courageous day! O most happy hour!
Bottom! Oh, most wonderful day! Oh, happiest hour!
Masters, I am to discourse wonders: but ask me not what; for if I tell / you, I am not true Athenian. I will tell you everything, right as it / fell out.
Gentlemen, I have wonders to tell you, but don't ask me what, because if I tell you, I'm no true Athenian. I'll tell you everything, exactly as it happened.

Not a word of me. All that I will tell you is, that the Duke hath / dined. Get your apparel together, good strings to your beards, new / ribbons to your pumps; meet presently at the palace; every man look / o'er his part. For the short and the long is, our play is preferred. In / any case, let Thisbe have clean linen; and let not him that plays the / lion pare his nails, for they shall hang out for the lion's claws. And / most dear actors, eat no onions nor garlick, for we are to utter sweet / breath; and I do not doubt but to hear them say it is a sweet comedy. / No more words. Away! Go, away!

Not a word from me. All I'll tell you is that the Duke has had his dinner. Get your costumes together, good strings for your beards, new ribbons for your shoes. Meet at the palace straight away. Every man, go over his part. Because the long and the short of it is, our play has been shortlisted. Anyway, make sure Thisbe has clean underclothes, and don't let the man playing the lion cut his nails, because they'll stick out as the lion's claws. And, dearest actors, don't eat onions or garlic, because we have to breathe sweet breath, and I'm sure we'll hear them say it's a sweet comedy. No more talking. Off you go! Go, off you go!
'Tis strange, my Theseus, that these lovers speak of.
These things the lovers are talking about are strange, my Theseus.

More strange than true. I never may believe / These antique fables, nor these fairy toys. / Lovers and madmen have such seething brains, / Such shaping fantasies, that apprehend / More than cool reason ever comprehends. / The lunatic, the lover, and the poet / Are of imagination all compact: / One sees more devils than vast hell can hold; / That is the madman: the lover, all as frantic, / Sees Helen's beauty in a brow of Egypt: / The poet's eye, in a fine frenzy rolling, / Doth glance from heaven to earth, from earth to heaven; / And as imagination bodies forth / The forms of things unknown, the poet's pen / Turns them to shapes, and gives to airy nothing / A local habitation and a name. / Such tricks hath strong imagination, / That if it would but apprehend some joy, / It comprehends some bringer of that joy. / Or in the night, imagining some fear, / How easy is a bush supposed a bear?

More strange than true. I can never believe these old legends or these silly fairy stories. Lovers and madmen have such boiling brains, such inventive imaginations, that they see more than calm reason can ever understand. The madman, the lover and the poet are all made entirely of imagination. One sees more devils than huge hell could hold: that's the madman. The lover, just as crazy, sees the beauty of Helen of Troy in a gypsy's face. The poet's eye, rolling in a fine frenzy, glances from heaven to earth and from earth to heaven, and as imagination gives body to things nobody knows, the poet's pen turns them into shapes and gives airy nothing a home and a name. Strong imagination plays such tricks that if it only feels some joy, it invents someone who brought that joy. Or at night, imagining something frightening, how easily a bush is taken for a bear!

But all the story of the night told over, / And all their minds transfigur'd so together, / More witnesseth than fancy's images, / And grows to something of great constancy; / But, howsoever, strange and admirable.

But the whole story of the night, as they tell it, and the way all their minds were changed together, proves it is more than imagination's pictures, and adds up to something very consistent. But, however it happened, it is strange and wonderful.
Here come the lovers, full of joy and mirth. / Joy, gentle friends, joy and fresh days of love / Accompany your hearts!
Here come the lovers, full of joy and happiness. Joy, gentle friends, joy and fresh days of love be with you!
More than to us / Wait in your royal walks, your board, your bed!
May even more joy than ours be with you on your royal walks, at your table and in your bed!

Come now; what masques, what dances shall we have, / To wear away this long age of three hours / Between our after-supper and bed-time? / Where is our usual manager of mirth? / What revels are in hand? Is there no play / To ease the anguish of a torturing hour? / Call Philostrate.

Come on now, what masques and dances shall we have to pass this endless age of three hours between after-supper and bedtime? Where is our usual master of entertainments? What shows are ready? Isn't there a play to ease the agony of a torturing hour? Call Philostrate.
Say, what abridgment have you for this evening? / What masque? What music? How shall we beguile / The lazy time, if not with some delight?
Tell me, what entertainment have you got to shorten this evening? What masque? What music? How shall we fool the lazy hours, if not with something enjoyable?
There is a brief how many sports are ripe. / Make choice of which your Highness will see first.
Here is a list of the entertainments that are ready. Choose which your Highness wants to see first.

[Reads] 'The battle with the Centaurs, to be sung / By an Athenian eunuch to the harp.' / We'll none of that. That have I told my love / In glory of my kinsman Hercules. / 'The riot of the tipsy Bacchanals, / Tearing the Thracian singer in their rage?' / That is an old device, and it was play'd / When I from Thebes came last a conqueror. / 'The thrice three Muses mourning for the death / Of learning, late deceas'd in beggary.' / That is some satire, keen and critical, / Not sorting with a nuptial ceremony. / 'A tedious brief scene of young Pyramus / And his love Thisbe; very tragical mirth.' / Merry and tragical? Tedious and brief? / That is hot ice and wondrous strange snow. / How shall we find the concord of this discord?

[He reads] 'The battle with the Centaurs, to be sung by an Athenian eunuch to the harp.' We won't have that. I've already told my love that story, in honour of my relative Hercules. 'The riot of the drunken followers of Bacchus, tearing Orpheus, the singer of Thrace, to pieces in their frenzy.' That's an old show. It was performed the last time I came back from Thebes as a conqueror. 'The nine Muses mourning the death of Learning, who recently died in poverty.' That's some satire, sharp and critical, not suitable for a wedding. 'A boring short scene of young Pyramus and his love Thisbe, very tragic comedy.' Comic and tragic? Boring and short? That's like hot ice and amazingly strange snow. How can we find harmony in this contradiction?

A play there is, my lord, some ten words long, / Which is as brief as I have known a play; / But by ten words, my lord, it is too long, / Which makes it tedious. For in all the play / There is not one word apt, one player fitted. / And tragical, my noble lord, it is. / For Pyramus therein doth kill himself, / Which, when I saw rehears'd, I must confess, / Made mine eyes water; but more merry tears / The passion of loud laughter never shed.

There is a play, my lord, about ten words long, which is as short as any play I've known. But it is ten words too long, my lord, which makes it boring, because in the whole play there isn't one word that's right, or one actor suited to his part. And it is tragic, my noble lord, because Pyramus kills himself in it. When I saw it rehearsed, I must admit, it made my eyes water, but no one ever cried happier tears from laughing out loud.
What are they that do play it?
Hard-handed men that work in Athens here, / Which never labour'd in their minds till now; / And now have toil'd their unbreath'd memories / With this same play against your nuptial.
Working men with rough hands, who work here in Athens and have never worked with their brains until now. And now they have strained their untrained memories learning this play for your wedding.

No, my noble lord, / It is not for you: I have heard it over, / And it is nothing, nothing in the world; / Unless you can find sport in their intents, / Extremely stretch'd and conn'd with cruel pain / To do you service.

No, my noble lord. It isn't good enough for you. I have heard it all the way through, and it is nothing, nothing at all, unless you can find amusement in their efforts, stretched to the limit and learned with terrible pain, to serve you.
I will hear that play; / For never anything can be amiss / When simpleness and duty tender it. / Go, bring them in: and take your places, ladies.
I will see that play, because nothing can ever be wrong when it is offered with simple honesty and a sense of duty. Go, bring them in. And take your seats, ladies.
I love not to see wretchedness o'ercharged, / And duty in his service perishing.
I don't like to see poor people overburdened, or their dutiful efforts falling flat.
Why, gentle sweet, you shall see no such thing.
Why, gentle sweetheart, you won't see anything like that.
He says they can do nothing in this kind.
He says they can't act at all.

The kinder we, to give them thanks for nothing. / Our sport shall be to take what they mistake: / And what poor duty cannot do, noble respect / Takes it in might, not merit. / Where I have come, great clerks have purposed / To greet me with premeditated welcomes; / Where I have seen them shiver and look pale, / Make periods in the midst of sentences, / Throttle their practis'd accent in their fears, / And, in conclusion, dumbly have broke off, / Not paying me a welcome. Trust me, sweet, / Out of this silence yet I pick'd a welcome; / And in the modesty of fearful duty / I read as much as from the rattling tongue / Of saucy and audacious eloquence. / Love, therefore, and tongue-tied simplicity / In least speak most to my capacity.

Then we are all the kinder to thank them for nothing. Our fun will be to accept their mistakes kindly. When poor, dutiful people can't do something well, a noble mind values the effort, not the result. Wherever I have been, great scholars have planned to greet me with prepared speeches of welcome. I've seen them tremble and go pale, stop in the middle of sentences, choke on their rehearsed words in fear, and in the end break off speechless, without welcoming me at all. Believe me, sweetheart, I still found a welcome in their silence, and in the modesty of their nervous duty I read as much as in the rattling tongue of cheeky, confident eloquence. So love and tongue-tied simplicity, saying least, say most to me.
So please your grace, the Prologue is address'd.
If it please your Grace, the Prologue is ready.

If we offend, it is with our good will. / That you should think, we come not to offend, / But with good will. To show our simple skill, / That is the true beginning of our end. / Consider then, we come but in despite. / We do not come, as minding to content you, / Our true intent is. All for your delight / We are not here. That you should here repent you, / The actors are at hand, and, by their show, / You shall know all that you are like to know.

If we offend, it is with our good will. That you should think we come not to offend, but with good will. To show our simple skill, that is the true beginning of our end. Think, then: we come only to spite you. We do not come intending to please you; that is our real aim. We are not here for your delight. That you should be sorry you came, the actors are ready, and by their show you'll learn all you are likely to learn. [Quince stops in all the wrong places, so every sentence says the opposite of what he means: that they come with good will, not to offend, and are here only to please.]
This fellow doth not stand upon points.
This man doesn't pay attention to his full stops.
He hath rid his prologue like a rough colt; he knows not the stop. A / good moral, my lord: it is not enough to speak, but to speak true.
He's ridden his prologue like a wild young horse: he doesn't know how to stop. That's a good lesson, my lord: it isn't enough to speak, you have to speak correctly.
Indeed he hath played on this prologue like a child on a recorder; a / sound, but not in government.
Yes, he's played this prologue like a child on a recorder: there's a sound, but no control.
His speech was like a tangled chain; nothing impaired, but all / disordered. Who is next?
His speech was like a tangled chain: no part broken, but all in a mess. Who's next?

Gentles, perchance you wonder at this show; / But wonder on, till truth make all things plain. / This man is Pyramus, if you would know; / This beauteous lady Thisbe is certain. / This man, with lime and rough-cast, doth present / Wall, that vile wall which did these lovers sunder; / And through Wall's chink, poor souls, they are content / To whisper, at the which let no man wonder. / This man, with lantern, dog, and bush of thorn, / Presenteth Moonshine, for, if you will know, / By moonshine did these lovers think no scorn / To meet at Ninus' tomb, there, there to woo. / This grisly beast (which Lion hight by name) / The trusty Thisbe, coming first by night, / Did scare away, or rather did affright; / And as she fled, her mantle she did fall; / Which Lion vile with bloody mouth did stain. / Anon comes Pyramus, sweet youth, and tall, / And finds his trusty Thisbe's mantle slain; / Whereat with blade, with bloody blameful blade, / He bravely broach'd his boiling bloody breast; / And Thisbe, tarrying in mulberry shade, / His dagger drew, and died. For all the rest, / Let Lion, Moonshine, Wall, and lovers twain, / At large discourse while here they do remain.

Ladies and gentlemen, maybe you're puzzled by this show, but keep wondering until the truth makes everything clear. This man is Pyramus, if you want to know. This beautiful lady is Thisbe, of course. This man, with plaster and gravel, represents Wall, that horrible wall which kept these lovers apart, and they are glad, poor things, to whisper through Wall's crack, which no one should be surprised at. This man, with a lantern, a dog and a bundle of thorn twigs, represents Moonshine, because, if you want to know, these lovers were not ashamed to meet by moonlight at Ninus's tomb, there, there to court each other. This horrible beast, who goes by the name of Lion, scared away, or rather frightened, faithful Thisbe when she arrived first at night. And as she ran away she dropped her cloak, which vile Lion stained with his bloody mouth. Soon Pyramus arrives, a sweet, tall young man, and finds his faithful Thisbe's cloak 'killed'. At this, with his blade, his bloody, blameworthy blade, he bravely broached his boiling, bloody breast. And Thisbe, waiting in the shade of the mulberry tree, drew his dagger and died. For all the rest, let Lion, Moonshine, Wall and the two lovers tell you everything while they're here.
I wonder if the lion be to speak.
I wonder whether the lion will speak.
No wonder, my lord. One lion may, when many asses do.
No wonder, my lord. One lion can speak when so many asses do.

In this same interlude it doth befall / That I, one Snout by name, present a wall: / And such a wall as I would have you think / That had in it a crannied hole or chink, / Through which the lovers, Pyramus and Thisbe, / Did whisper often very secretly. / This loam, this rough-cast, and this stone, doth show / That I am that same wall; the truth is so: / And this the cranny is, right and sinister, / Through which the fearful lovers are to whisper.

In this same play it happens that I, Snout by name, play a wall, and the sort of wall, I'd like you to think, that had a cracked hole or chink in it, through which the lovers Pyramus and Thisbe often whispered very secretly. This clay, this plaster and this stone show that I am that same wall. That's the truth. And this is the crack, right and left, through which the frightened lovers are going to whisper.
Would you desire lime and hair to speak better?
Could you want plaster and horsehair to speak any better?
It is the wittiest partition that ever I heard discourse, my lord.
It's the cleverest wall I ever heard give a speech, my lord.
Pyramus draws near the wall; silence.
Pyramus is coming to the wall. Quiet.

O grim-look'd night! O night with hue so black! / O night, which ever art when day is not! / O night, O night, alack, alack, alack, / I fear my Thisbe's promise is forgot! / And thou, O wall, O sweet, O lovely wall, / That stand'st between her father's ground and mine; / Thou wall, O wall, O sweet and lovely wall, / Show me thy chink, to blink through with mine eyne.

Oh grim-looking night! Oh night so black in colour! Oh night, which always is when day is not! Oh night, oh night, alas, alas, alas, I fear my Thisbe has forgotten her promise! And you, oh wall, oh sweet, oh lovely wall, that stands between her father's land and mine, you wall, oh wall, oh sweet and lovely wall, show me your crack, so I can peep through with my eyes.
Thanks, courteous wall: Jove shield thee well for this! / But what see I? No Thisbe do I see. / O wicked wall, through whom I see no bliss, / Curs'd be thy stones for thus deceiving me!
Thank you, polite wall. Jove protect you for this! But what do I see? No Thisbe do I see. Oh wicked wall, through which I see no happiness, curse your stones for tricking me like this!
The wall, methinks, being sensible, should curse again.
I think the wall, since it can feel, should curse him back.
No, in truth, sir, he should not. 'Deceiving me' is Thisbe's cue: she / is to enter now, and I am to spy her through the wall. You shall see it / will fall pat as I told you. Yonder she comes.
No, honestly, sir, he shouldn't. 'Tricking me' is Thisbe's cue. She comes on now, and I have to spot her through the wall. You'll see, it'll happen exactly as I told you. Here she comes.
O wall, full often hast thou heard my moans, / For parting my fair Pyramus and me. / My cherry lips have often kiss'd thy stones, / Thy stones with lime and hair knit up in thee.
Oh wall, you have very often heard me moan because you keep my handsome Pyramus and me apart. My cherry lips have often kissed your stones, your stones stuck together with plaster and hair.
I see a voice; now will I to the chink, / To spy an I can hear my Thisbe's face. / Thisbe?
I see a voice! Now I'll go to the crack to see if I can hear my Thisbe's face. Thisbe?
My love thou art, my love I think.
You are my love, my love I think.
Think what thou wilt, I am thy lover's grace; / And like Limander am I trusty still.
Think what you like, I am your gracious lover, and like Limander I am still faithful.
And I like Helen, till the fates me kill.
And I'm like Helen, until the Fates kill me.
Not Shafalus to Procrus was so true.
Shafalus was never so true to Procrus.
As Shafalus to Procrus, I to you.
As Shafalus was to Procrus, so am I to you.
O kiss me through the hole of this vile wall.
Oh, kiss me through the hole in this vile wall!
I kiss the wall's hole, not your lips at all.
