I'm kissing the wall's hole, not your lips at all.
Wilt thou at Ninny's tomb meet me straightway?
Will you meet me at Ninny's tomb straight away?
'Tide life, 'tide death, I come without delay.
Come life or come death, I'll come without delay.
Thus have I, Wall, my part discharged so; / And, being done, thus Wall away doth go.
So I, Wall, have played my part, and now it's done, Wall goes away.
Now is the mural down between the two neighbours.
Now the wall between the two neighbours is down.
No remedy, my lord, when walls are so wilful to hear without warning.
There's no help for it, my lord, when walls are so keen to listen without warning.
This is the silliest stuff that ever I heard.
This is the silliest nonsense I've ever heard.
The best in this kind are but shadows; and the worst are no worse, if / imagination amend them.
The best plays of this kind are only shadows, and the worst are no worse, if imagination improves them.
It must be your imagination then, and not theirs.
Then it must be your imagination that does it, not theirs.
If we imagine no worse of them than they of themselves, they may pass / for excellent men. Here come two noble beasts in, a man and a lion.
If we think no worse of them than they think of themselves, they could pass for excellent men. Here come two noble beasts, a man and a lion.

You, ladies, you, whose gentle hearts do fear / The smallest monstrous mouse that creeps on floor, / May now, perchance, both quake and tremble here, / When lion rough in wildest rage doth roar. / Then know that I, one Snug the joiner, am / A lion fell, nor else no lion's dam; / For if I should as lion come in strife / Into this place, 'twere pity on my life.

You ladies, whose gentle hearts are frightened of the smallest monstrous mouse that creeps across the floor, may now perhaps shake and tremble here, when a rough lion roars in wildest rage. So know that I, Snug the joiner, am a fierce lion only in costume, and no lioness either. Because if I came into this place as a real lion looking for a fight, I'd be sorry for my life.
A very gentle beast, and of a good conscience.
A very gentle beast, with a good conscience.
The very best at a beast, my lord, that e'er I saw.
The best at playing a beast I ever saw, my lord.
This lion is a very fox for his valour.
This lion is a real fox when it comes to bravery.
True; and a goose for his discretion.
True, and a goose when it comes to good sense.
Not so, my lord, for his valour cannot carry his discretion, and the / fox carries the goose.
Not so, my lord, because his bravery can't carry off his good sense, and a fox carries off a goose.
His discretion, I am sure, cannot carry his valour; for the goose / carries not the fox. It is well; leave it to his discretion, and let us / listen to the moon.
I'm sure his good sense can't carry off his bravery, because a goose doesn't carry off a fox. Well, leave it to his good sense, and let's listen to the moon.
This lanthorn doth the hornèd moon present.
This lantern represents the horned moon.
He should have worn the horns on his head.
He should have worn the horns on his head.
He is no crescent, and his horns are invisible within the / circumference.
He isn't a crescent moon, and his horns are invisible inside his full circle.
This lanthorn doth the hornèd moon present; / Myself the man i' the moon do seem to be.
This lantern represents the horned moon. I seem to be the man in the moon.
This is the greatest error of all the rest; the man should be put into / the lantern. How is it else the man i' the moon?
That's the biggest mistake of all. The man should be put inside the lantern. How else is he the man in the moon?
He dares not come there for the candle, for you see, it is already in / snuff.
He doesn't dare go in there because of the candle. You see, it's already burning badly.
I am aweary of this moon. Would he would change!
I'm tired of this moon. I wish he would change!
It appears by his small light of discretion that he is in the wane; but / yet, in courtesy, in all reason, we must stay the time.
Judging by his feeble light of good sense, he seems to be waning. But still, to be polite, and fair, we must wait it out.
All that I have to say, is to tell you that the lantern is the moon; I / the man i' the moon; this thorn-bush my thorn-bush; and this dog my / dog.
All I have to say is to tell you that the lantern is the moon, I am the man in the moon, this thorn bush is my thorn bush, and this dog is my dog.
Why, all these should be in the lantern, for all these are in the moon. / But silence; here comes Thisbe.
Well, all these should be in the lantern, because they're all in the moon. But quiet, here comes Thisbe.
This is old Ninny's tomb. Where is my love?
This is old Ninny's tomb. Where is my love?
Well shone, Moon. Truly, the moon shines with a good grace.
Well shone, Moon. Honestly, the moon shines very nicely.
Well mauled, Lion, like a cat with a mouse.

Sweet Moon, I thank thee for thy sunny beams; / I thank thee, Moon, for shining now so bright; / For, by thy gracious golden, glittering gleams, / I trust to take of truest Thisbe sight. / But stay! O spite! / But mark, poor knight, / What dreadful dole is here! / Eyes, do you see? / How can it be? / O dainty duck! O dear! / Thy mantle good, / What, stained with blood? / Approach, ye Furies fell! / O Fates, come, come; / Cut thread and thrum; / Quail, rush, conclude, and quell!

Sweet Moon, I thank you for your sunny beams. I thank you, Moon, for shining so brightly now, because by your gracious, golden, glittering gleams I hope to get a sight of my most faithful Thisbe. But wait! Oh, cruel! But look, poor knight, what dreadful grief is here! Eyes, do you see? How can it be? Oh dainty duck! Oh dear! Your good cloak, what, stained with blood? Come here, you cruel Furies! Oh Fates, come, come, cut the thread of my life, thread and fringe, crush, destroy, finish and kill!
This passion, and the death of a dear friend, would go near to make a / man look sad.
This grief, together with the death of a dear friend, would almost make a man look sad.
Beshrew my heart, but I pity the man.
Curse my heart, but I feel sorry for the man.

O wherefore, Nature, didst thou lions frame, / Since lion vile hath here deflower'd my dear? / Which is—no, no—which was the fairest dame / That liv'd, that lov'd, that lik'd, that look'd with cheer. / Come, tears, confound! / Out, sword, and wound / The pap of Pyramus; / Ay, that left pap, / Where heart doth hop: / Thus die I, thus, thus, thus. / Now am I dead, / Now am I fled; / My soul is in the sky. / Tongue, lose thy light! / Moon, take thy flight! / Now die, die, die, die, die.

Oh, why, Nature, did you make lions, since a vile lion has 'deflowered' my dear here? She is (no, no) she was the most beautiful lady who ever lived, loved, liked, or looked cheerful. Come, tears, destroy me! Out, sword, and wound the breast of Pyramus. Yes, that left breast, where the heart hops. So I die, like this, this, this. Now I am dead, now I have fled, my soul is in the sky. Tongue, lose your light! Moon, fly away! Now die, die, die, die, die.
No die, but an ace, for him; for he is but one.
Not a dice but an ace for him, because he's only one.
Less than an ace, man; for he is dead, he is nothing.
Less than an ace, man, because he's dead. He's nothing.
With the help of a surgeon he might yet recover and prove an ass.
With the help of a surgeon he might still recover and turn out to be an ass.
How chance Moonshine is gone before Thisbe comes back and finds her / lover?
How come Moonshine has gone before Thisbe comes back and finds her lover?
She will find him by starlight.
Here she comes, and her passion ends the play.
Here she comes, and her grief will end the play.
Methinks she should not use a long one for such a Pyramus. I hope she / will be brief.
I don't think she should make a long speech of grief for such a Pyramus. I hope she'll be brief.
A mote will turn the balance, which Pyramus, which Thisbe, is the / better: he for a man, God warrant us; she for a woman, God bless us!
A speck of dust would tip the scales over which is better, Pyramus or Thisbe: he as a man, God help us, or she as a woman, God bless us!
She hath spied him already with those sweet eyes.
She's already spotted him with those sweet eyes.
And so she moans, as follows...

Asleep, my love? / What, dead, my dove? / O Pyramus, arise, / Speak, speak. Quite dumb? / Dead, dead? A tomb / Must cover thy sweet eyes. / These lily lips, / This cherry nose, / These yellow cowslip cheeks, / Are gone, are gone! / Lovers, make moan; / His eyes were green as leeks. / O Sisters Three, / Come, come to me, / With hands as pale as milk; / Lay them in gore, / Since you have shore / With shears his thread of silk. / Tongue, not a word: / Come, trusty sword, / Come, blade, my breast imbrue; / And farewell, friends. / Thus Thisbe ends. / Adieu, adieu, adieu.

Asleep, my love? What, dead, my dove? Oh Pyramus, get up! Speak, speak. Quite silent? Dead, dead? A tomb must cover your sweet eyes. These lily-white lips, this cherry-red nose, these yellow cowslip cheeks are gone, are gone! Lovers, moan. His eyes were as green as leeks. Oh Three Sisters of Fate, come, come to me with hands as pale as milk. Dip them in blood, since you have cut his silken thread of life with your scissors. Tongue, not a word. Come, trusty sword. Come, blade, soak my breast in blood. And farewell, friends. This is how Thisbe ends. Goodbye, goodbye, goodbye.
Moonshine and Lion are left to bury the dead.
Moonshine and Lion are left to bury the dead.
No, I assure you; the wall is down that parted their fathers. Will it / please you to see the epilogue, or to hear a Bergomask dance between / two of our company?
No, I promise you, the wall that separated their fathers has come down. Would you like to see the epilogue, or hear a country dance performed by two of our company?

No epilogue, I pray you; for your play needs no excuse. Never excuse; / for when the players are all dead there need none to be blamed. Marry, / if he that writ it had played Pyramus, and hanged himself in Thisbe's / garter, it would have been a fine tragedy; and so it is, truly; and / very notably discharged. But come, your Bergomask; let your epilogue / alone.

No epilogue, please, because your play needs no apology. Never apologise, because when the actors are all dead, no one needs to be blamed. Really, if the man who wrote it had played Pyramus and hanged himself with Thisbe's garter, it would have been a fine tragedy. And so it is, truly, and very remarkably performed. But come on, your country dance. Forget the epilogue.

The iron tongue of midnight hath told twelve. / Lovers, to bed; 'tis almost fairy time. / I fear we shall outsleep the coming morn / As much as we this night have overwatch'd. / This palpable-gross play hath well beguil'd / The heavy gait of night. Sweet friends, to bed. / A fortnight hold we this solemnity / In nightly revels and new jollity.

The iron tongue of the midnight bell has struck twelve. Lovers, to bed. It's almost fairy time. I'm afraid we'll sleep late into the morning, as long as we've stayed up tonight. This obviously crude play has helped the slow night pass very well. Sweet friends, to bed. For two weeks we'll keep up this celebration with parties every night and new festivities.

Now the hungry lion roars, / And the wolf behowls the moon; / Whilst the heavy ploughman snores, / All with weary task fordone. / Now the wasted brands do glow, / Whilst the screech-owl, screeching loud, / Puts the wretch that lies in woe / In remembrance of a shroud. / Now it is the time of night / That the graves, all gaping wide, / Every one lets forth his sprite, / In the church-way paths to glide. / And we fairies, that do run / By the triple Hecate's team / From the presence of the sun, / Following darkness like a dream, / Now are frolic; not a mouse / Shall disturb this hallow'd house. / I am sent with broom before, / To sweep the dust behind the door.

Now the hungry lion roars and the wolf howls at the moon, while the tired ploughman snores, worn out by his hard work. Now the burnt-out logs glow, while the screech owl, screeching loudly, makes the miserable person lying ill think of his burial shroud. Now it is the time of night when the graves all gape wide, and every one lets out its ghost to glide along the paths to the church. And we fairies, who run beside the chariot of Hecate, goddess of the moon and the underworld, away from the sun, following darkness like a dream, are now ready for fun. Not a mouse will disturb this blessed house. I've been sent ahead with a broom to sweep the dust from behind the door.
Through the house give glimmering light, / By the dead and drowsy fire. / Every elf and fairy sprite / Hop as light as bird from brier, / And this ditty after me, / Sing and dance it trippingly.
Give a flickering light through the house from the dying, sleepy fire. Every elf and fairy spirit, hop as lightly as a bird from a briar, and sing this song after me and dance it nimbly.
First rehearse your song by rote, / To each word a warbling note; / Hand in hand, with fairy grace, / Will we sing, and bless this place.
First, practise your song by heart, with a trilling note for every word. Hand in hand, with fairy grace, we'll sing and bless this place.

Now, until the break of day, / Through this house each fairy stray. / To the best bride-bed will we, / Which by us shall blessèd be; / And the issue there create / Ever shall be fortunate. / So shall all the couples three / Ever true in loving be; / And the blots of Nature's hand / Shall not in their issue stand: / Never mole, hare-lip, nor scar, / Nor mark prodigious, such as are / Despised in nativity, / Shall upon their children be. / With this field-dew consecrate, / Every fairy take his gait, / And each several chamber bless, / Through this palace, with sweet peace; / And the owner of it blest. / Ever shall it in safety rest, / Trip away. Make no stay; / Meet me all by break of day.

Now, until daybreak, let every fairy wander through this house. We will go to the best bridal bed, which we will bless, and the children made there will always be lucky. So all three couples will always be faithful in love, and Nature's flaws will not appear in their children. No mole, cleft lip or scar, no unnatural birthmark of the kind people hate to see in a newborn baby, will be on their children. With this blessed dew from the fields, let every fairy go on its way and bless each room in this palace with sweet peace, and bless the owner too. It will always rest in safety. Skip away. Don't stay. Meet me, all of you, by daybreak.

If we shadows have offended, / Think but this, and all is mended, / That you have but slumber'd here / While these visions did appear. / And this weak and idle theme, / No more yielding but a dream, / Gentles, do not reprehend. / If you pardon, we will mend. / And, as I am an honest Puck, / If we have unearnèd luck / Now to 'scape the serpent's tongue, / We will make amends ere long; / Else the Puck a liar call. / So, good night unto you all. / Give me your hands, if we be friends, / And Robin shall restore amends.

If we shadows have offended you, just think this, and everything is put right: that you have only been asleep here while these visions appeared. And this weak and silly story, which is no more than a dream, ladies and gentlemen, don't criticise it. If you forgive us, we'll do better. And as I am an honest Puck, if we are lucky enough, though we don't deserve it, to escape your hisses, we'll make it up to you soon, or else call Puck a liar. So, good night to you all. Give me your applause, if we're friends, and Robin will make amends.
